This study examines the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks applied to determining the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube. Under the assumption that the ground state resides in the spectral Barron space, we demonstrate that even as dimensions increase, the generalization error remains bounded in the high-dimensional limit. The result is supported by a dimension-independent lower bound on approximation accuracy, achieved using networks with weights of optimal magnitude. Furthermore, the paper addresses any non-zero spectral gap in the associated eigenvalue spectrum.

This study examines the directional distribution of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory, focusing on events with energy levels exceeding 8 EeV. Analysis covers the full dataset collected between April 2004 and December 2014, comprising 4,912 such events. The investigation reveals no indications of isotropy; instead, significant anisotropies were detected when comparing the observed distribution against simulations based on both an isotropic model and one accounting for source localization within the Galactic Plane (GP). Specifically, a preferred direction $(-55^{\circ}, 15^{\circ})$ in Galactic coordinates was identified, showing significant probability ($p < 0.01$) of alignment with both a Galactic source distribution and the previously noted preferred direction. Furthermore, a clustering effect is evident near the Galactic Center ($0^{\circ}, 0^{\circ}$), with similar significance levels ($p < 0.01$). These findings were reinforced by analyzing the $5^{\circ} \times 5^{\circ}$ box centered on each location, where observed probabilities of alignment reached $p < 0.003$ for aligned sources and $p < 0.005$ for an assumed uniform GP distribution.

This study examines the global behavior of spin-1/2 particle semilinear equations under the influence of electromagnetic fields within the Lorentz framework. Building upon an earlier study by J. Es-Saadi, this paper establishes the existence of global solutions for the general case, with or without the Lorentz condition as imposed by Lochak and Majorana. Specifically, a unique global solution $u \in C^{1}[0, +\infty)[, H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})]$ is proven to exist and remain complete on the interval $[0, +\infty)$ initially within the $H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ space, assuming initial data in this space. Furthermore, precise quantitative estimates for the $L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$ norm of the solution over time are derived.

This paper details an open-source end-to-end deep learning framework for analyzing histopathology images, with a specific focus on creating a segmentation model to delimit tissue regions. Our primary objective is to develop this segmenter using federated learning (FL), a technique that aggregates deep learning data across multiple independent institutions. Such a federated approach addresses critical challenges in traditional data sharing, including privacy concerns, regulatory hurdles, and the costs associated with transferring data. We have created the Tissue-level Segmentation End-ToEnd (TISE) pipeline, which supports FL across the entire end-to-end machine learning process.

Cavity magnomechanical fields are attracting significant interest for generating large magnon-mechanphonon interactions through engineering a nonlinearity induced by springs. In this study, we show via theoretical analysis that a similar enhancement can be achieved through nonlinear coupling between phonons and magnons. This suggests that both mechanical components—the mechanical element in cavity magnomechanics and those in spring-induced mechanisms—are not essential; instead, direct nonlinear coupling can be intrinsic to the material itself. This idea is substantiated by demonstrations of a tunable Josephson bifrquillator using yttrium iron garnet (YIG), which exhibits strong group-mechanically phonons due to its electrostriction. These results advance understanding of how to leverage YIG's inherent coupling properties to improve future devices.

Super-massive black holes (SMBHs), which range from $10^6$ to $10^9$ solar masses, are prevalent throughout the universe today, with particularly close attention drawn to low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs). These objects possess accretion rates that are too high to be merely accreting gas in radiatively inefficient modes, yet emit far less than their expected luminosity based on that accretion rate. Consequently, their physical mechanisms remain a subject of intense scientific debate. This paper introduces a novel model-free redesign approach for controllers in closed-loop systems utilizing reinforcement learning (RL). Since traditional RL relies solely on trial-and-error to enhance control performance, resulting in potentially suboptimal outcomes or failed learning convergence, the proposed method enhances this process by incorporating heuristics. By leveraging system models and insights from control theory to guide the RL algorithm, the technique allows for more reliable and substantially faster convergence to near-optimal solutions. Fundamentals of the theoretical underpinnings and convergence of the strategy are explored. Subsequently, the paper highlights the synthesis of a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) based on the modified value iteration algorithm. Subsequent simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of this model-based RL approach when contrasted with standard model-free implementations.

The SiD Detector, which was investigated at the SLAC Linear Collider (linear accelerator at SLA) for hadron collisions now proceeding to the design phase. A key feature of this detector is its innovative radial-drift time-of-flight system, which, in conjunction with a robust magnetic spectrometer and precise tracking resolution, ensures excellent momentum analysis (around 10^-3 GeV) for particles. The robust magnetic spectrometer, which is designed with a flat, "pancake" shape using a magnetic field of around 11 Tesla, allows for excellent analysis of the magnetic field. The tracking resolution, which is around 10^-3 m, ensures accurate analysis of the magnetic field. The analysis of the magnetic field, which is around 11.5 m, ensures that the detector can analyze the magnetic field with high precision.

We report the discovery of Tonozintla 2 (Ton2), a newly identified Milky Way globular cluster located within the Galactic halo, based on *Gaia* DR3 data. This catalogues-driven discovery utilized specific selection criteria to compile a list of candidate objects. Initial photometric and spectroscopic verification confirmed Ton2 as a distinct cluster. Its position in the galaxy is determined to be approximately 17.5 kiloparsecs from the galactic center, with a distance modulus of roughly 14.08 mag. Analysis of variable stars reveals Ton2 hosts four pulsating members: three exhibiting large-amplitude pulsations and one small-amplitude star. Notably, two of the large-amplitude stars and one small-amplitude star show signs of significant nitrogen enrichment. This phenomenon is typically linked to mass transfer from a binary companion that once underwent the third-mixing phase in a post-main-sequence star. The presence of these enriched stars provides compelling evidence that multiple stellar populations exist within Ton2. Furthermore, a detailed asteroseismic investigation of one of these enriched pulsators, Ton2-LAS-1, was conducted. This study identifies 16 frequency peaks and models the star using standard oscillation modes (g and p modes). The resulting seismic parameters yield a core helium fraction of 0.392 and an envelope helium fraction of 0.022. Monitoring the state of the Earth and its ecosystems is vital for addressing global challenges, such as managing urban areas, forests, and controlling pollution. Consequently, the demand for high-resolution Earth observation (EO) data is increasing, supported by numerous satellites deployed by both government agencies and space commercial entities. These satellites generate vast quantities of imagery, necessitating robust data curation and management (DMM) systems. Although several such systems exist, they often lack support for distributed datasets and detailed metadata, frequently requiring costly hardware upgrades and custom software development. This paper introduces DMT, an open, flexible data management framework designed specifically for Earth observation datasets. DMT leverages semantic Web technologies, including RDF, OWL, and SPARQL, to manage data and metadata across heterogeneous sources using standard formats. By adopting a distributed architecture, DMT enables the integrated, queryable handling of diverse information without centralization, ensuring compatibility with other data handlers through adherance to these semantic standards.

We derive the coarse-grained dynamical equations governing the elastic deformations of a 2D active nematic on which square-shaped colloidal particles are aligned perpendicular to the hydrodynamic flow. After confirming the stability of the resulting static static configurations, we identify a marginal case: the equations of motion exhibit a subtle dependence on scale by a quadratic term. This suggests the dynamic equations are marginally nonlinear. We then investigate the collective modes within an orthogonal strip geometry, finding that the added nonlinearity modifies the dispersion relation only at very large length scales. Furthermore, we examine the systems response to large initial distortions and find that the magnitude of viscoelastic relaxation times—ranging from micrometers to centimeters—depends critically on the strength of the marginally irrelevant quadratic term in the governing equations.

Detecting spatio-temporal anomalies in urban environments is crucial for diverse industries, yet current approaches relying on dense sensor networks face significant hurdles including prohibitive costs, slow deployment, and inadequate scalability. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces SpANet, a novel deep learning framework designed to identify spatio-temporal anomalies using sparse data. This model incorporates a Saliency Map for robust pre-training and an Attention mechanism to refine feature extraction, alongside a new loss function and data augmentation techniques specifically for handling suppression values. Experimental results show that SpANet outperforms existing state-of-the-art models across multiple benchmarks.

The research utilizes a high-luminity $e^+e-$ data sample ($\sqrt{s}=1.02$ GeV) collected by the BESIII detector. The analysis method involves a $\chi^2$ fit to identify peaks in the $\pi\pi$ invariant mass spectrum, allowing for the extraction of branching ratios. While capable of leveraging vast datasets, learning these features is computationally costly and the resulting representations are inefficient for storage and computation. In contrast, our proposed graph-based model encile the binary outcome directly from code structure using a neural network trained on two variables for binary source lines: the variable count and line length. We present the first stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) specifically for early-type galaxies (ETGs), derived from nearly 1,000 data points sourced from 14 diverse literature studies. Our analysis reveals two distinct segments within the SHMR: the slope is significantly gentler for massive ETGs ($M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{10.5} M_{\odot}$) than for less early ones, peaking near a stellar mass of approximately $10^{10.9} M_{\odot}$. This peak aligns precisely with the peak stellar mass density located at the virial center of galaxy halos, suggesting that the most massive ETGs form via the accretion of smaller precursors situated at virial center. Additionally, our findings indicate that the ETG SHMR is consistently flatter than that observed for late-type galaxies (LTGs) across the entire mass range. This distinction implies that the primary formation channels for ETGs and LTGs differ fundamentally.

This study introduces a technique to eliminate the influence of the stellar point spread function (PSF) on the vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) derived from stellar photometry. While VAOD offers a cost-effective means of monitoring atmospheric clarity using public astronomy data, it typically suffers from a ceiling on precision due to the necessity of simultaneous measurements at two distinct altitudes. Although PSF variations with altitude form the largest source of uncertainty, the proposed algorithm significantly mitigates this factor, yielding results that align closely with those from the classical method. The algorithm's validity is confirmed through simulations and validation against the public MMT Observatory dataset, ensuring its accuracy.

The Graphical Lasso methodology, first proposed by Friedman et al. in 2008, remains the standard current statistical procedure for estimating sparse precision matrices. Although computationally efficient, this original algorithm lacks guaranteed bounds regarding numerical accuracy. This study introduces a reformulated objective function that supports the development of $\epsilon$-near-optimal sparse solutions within polynomial time. We establish the computational complexity of applying the graphical Lasso approach to graphical models ranging from sparse to dense structures. Furthermore, this framework paves the way for verifying solution precision in graphical analysis and has significant implications for machine learning, where exact solutions are often unnecessary; in such contexts, possessing known approximation bounds is critically important.

This study utilizes 1-10 μm archival Spitzer archival data from an ACACIA survey targeting the TW Hydrae Association to create a comprehensive deconvolved spectral energy distribution (SED) for the first time. By comparing these observations with radiative transfer models, we identify that photoevaporation drives the scattered light seen in FOSSES/Infrared Spectrograph (FIPS) images and emission in the 10 μm band, while photophorescence likely accounts for the 4.5 μm emission. Our analysis indicates that a photoevaporation-driven wind, originating from a low-mass accretion disk, successfully explains the multi-wavelength SED across all Telescopium observations. Furthermore, the inferred photoevaporation rate, estimated at approximately $10^{-9} M_\odot / yr$, is significantly higher than what would be generated by stellar radiation alone, suggesting an additional, unidentified source of disk heating.

Detecting voiced speech, estimating the fundamental frequency, and continuously tracking pitch over time are vital components of numerous speech processing methodologies, such as voice activity detection, automatic speech recognition, and musical source separation. In this paper, we introduce three novel deep learning models designed for the challenging task of identifying voiced speech segments on mono acoustic signals, specifically targeting low-bitrate and low-sample-rate conditions encountered in remote microphones. These techniques, which rely solely on compressed audio inputs, significantly outperform conventional methods by orders of magnitude across a wide spectrum of scenarios.

We introduce a new Dynamically Weighted Inertial Forward-Backward (DWIFOB) algorithm designed to address monotone inclusion problems. This proposal builds upon the globally convergent forward-backward framework of forward steps defined by Adly et al. [J. Conv. Anal., 2019], the subsequent backward step corrected by them for convexity assurance, and corresponding forward predictive inertial steps. Drawing inspiration from various globally convergent inertial forward-backward methods in the literature, the specific weighting function introduced by our proposal enables convergence to all solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that selecting the weighting function within certain constraints yields asymptotic convergence rates matching those achieved by non-convergent algorithms. In addition, we present a vDFB algorithm derived from our primary proposal and establish its global convergence to all solutions with an optimal rate. We also provide numerical experiments showing that a primal-dual variant of our algorithm outperforms both the standard Chambolle-Pock method and another globally convergent forward-backward approach. Finally, we detail the application of these methodologies to the restoration of a degraded text using a specific optimization model.

We examine a theoretical model where non-zero, minute neutrino masses emerge via the radiative mechanism, operating under conditions that the lepton parity is broken by the dynamical formation of a chiral condensate between muons and taus. The lepton parity-breaking muon-aut boson (or similar) interaction generates charged boson masses through autome-dian fermion self-coupling, preventing the advent of Z bosals, while the same mechanism protects the naturalness of the a-tau condensate against the same radiative corrections. The authors also explore how the model can be tested experimentally.

Recent advancements in neural architecture search (NAS) within machine learning have fueled interest in using neural networks for other computational tasks. However, current deep-learning-based approaches often explore complex, complex genotypes, creating heavy computational burdens that prevent the training of practical performance models on complete search spaces. While black-box optimization of search spaces is under-explored in machine learning, this paper demonstrates the feasibility of using neural networks to model abstract search spaces effectively by focusing on neural abstract syntax graphs. We introduce Neural Architecture Synthesis, a method that trains a model on abstract representations to predict the relative performance of models within an entire design space, reducing evaluation cost from $\mathcal{O}(N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$. Experimental results show our proposed optimizers discover high-performing models far faster than established black-box baselines, while a new proposed black-box method leverages neural synthesis for faster convergence. These findings highlight two key contributions: (1) neural models can successfully learn abstract performance spaces, and (2), when space reduction techniques like genotypic pruning are applied, these models outperform black-box methods significantly in convergence speed.

Multicast beamforming is essential for enhancing spectral efficiency in future wireless networks, yet determining the optimal multigroup formation remains a challenging non-convex problem due to the complex coupling between group assignments and beamforming strategies. This paper addresses downlink scenarios where a base station with multiple antennas must form multiple groups to maximize the total downlink sum rate using the cardinality of various groups as criteria. A primary innovation of our approach is the simultaneous optimization of group selection and multicast beamforming vectors. The associated joint design problem has been proven non-convex; therefore, an iterative algorithm is developed through the alternating minimization of these variables. Specifically, the group selection subproblem is modeled using a binary integer linear program (BILP) and solved via a branch-and-bound method, while the beamforming subproblem is solved via second-order conic programming (SOCP). Comprehensive simulations are performed to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed design.

Communication efficiency is a critical factor for practical deployments of Federated Learning (FL). This paper proposes Distillation as a new framework to enhance FL communications. At each communication round, only a single model update is transmitted from the server to clients, contrasting sharply with multiple required transmissions in standard FL protocols. Additionally, at the client level, Distillation transmits fewer neural network weights than conventional FL learning. Specifically, a client performs local parameter updates using distilled knowledge from multiple distillation models derived from the central server, which are generated using the aggregated global parameters. We validate the efficacy of this approach on standard FL communication setups using two key metrics: the number of client-side communications and the clients-side transmitted data volume per local update. Experiments conducted on two real-world datasets, CIFAR-10 and Fin-gesture, demonstrate that Communication Distillation significantly boosts efficiency. The method achieves a 3× to 8× (or up to 3.8×) reduction in the number of client communications and a 2.6× (or up to 3.8×) decrease in the amount of data transmitted locally, all while maintaining comparable model performance compared to traditional FL.

Named Data Networking (NDN) represents an information-centric approach to next-generation service applications within distributed computing networks. The network architecture is organized into three primary planes: control, data, and management. The NCC module, situated within the control plane, serves as the network controller and manages the network state by regulating all devices and application entities. Utilizing the management module in conjunction with the network state machine, NCC dynamically generates and disseminates a network-wide state for subsequent processing. The NCC module also handles incoming requests, whether local or remote, and manages request forwarding. The paper details the internal structure of NCC along with its core functionalities. Furthermore, the internal operations of these functionalities are managed by a software framework designed to support a network-wide implementation of a centralized or distributed state. Finally, the paper introduces key findings from an experimental evaluation of NCC using the single-hop RIT NCC prototype.

This research addresses the unresolved issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler–Bernoulli beam on a metric graph structured as a non-star-shaped graph with one vertex and one external loop. For a specific range of physical parameters, the study derives precise necessary and sufficient conditions regarding the graph's geometry and these parameters regarding exponential stability. It establishes that within the system's solution set, eigenvectors exist that optimize the stability index; this optimization occurs either by minimizing the stability index itself or, equivalently, by maximizing it to achieve the most rapid decay. Consequently, the proposed conditions link the system-specific geometric features directly to stability properties. The theoretical framework relies primarily on an innovative approach involving eigenvectors constructed with support confined to individual graph edges.

This study examines whether inhomogeneous chiral phases exist within the quark-meson model, which incorporates explicit chiral-symmetry breaking. Results indicate that although the region permitting these inhomogeneities diminishes as pion mass increases, such phases persist at the physical pion mass. Furthermore, instability driving inhomogeneous matter formation manifests in the scalar channel, as opposed to the less favorable pseudoscalar modes.

The topological properties of the superconductor Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ have been the subject of extensive study and debate for years. Our angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) findings reveal that this material experiences a robust $s$-$p$ band inversion near the Fermi level ($E_F$), a phenomenon driven by electron-electron interactions which shift the $2p$-derived band upward toward $E_F$. Identifying this band inversion is crucial, as it confirms the electron-electron correlation effects observed in similar topological materials like BiSe and SbSe. Recognizing the unique $s$-$p$ band character of Sr$_2$RuO$_4$ offers new insights into its complex superconducting mechanism.

Current multi-objective optimization approaches typically rely on either predefined utility functions or interactive methods that gather expert preferences to identify the subset of optimal solutions. However, relying on utility functions is problematic because the true function is often unknown, and gathering preferences is inefficient as it does not always effectively narrow down a vast Pareto front. Furthermore, these interaction-heavy paradigms demand frequent user input, which becomes impractical in scenarios involving complex utility assessments. This work introduces RULOO, a system designed to handle both simple and intricate objective functions by utilizing large Language Models (LLMs) for preference learning without requiring direct user involvement. Specifically, an LLM analyzes the consequences of actions across multiple dimensions to compare any two scenarios, thereby establishing preferences that remain consistent even when the underlying concepts are complicated. RULOB merges this preference-driven strategy with preference theorem reasoning; by applying logical theorems to infer preferences for unvisited state comparisons, the method avoids unnecessary interactions. Extensive experiments comparing RULOB against state-of-the-art baselines using synthetic and real-world cases demonstrate superior performance, whether employing explicit or implicit input from experts.

Recent studies have demonstrated that machine learning models can be deceived using adversarial samples; however, the impact of such inputs on reinforcement learning agents within control tasks remains uncertain. In this study, we investigate potential vulnerabilities by employing on-policy and off-policy methods to train agents for the Atari game Pong while introducing generated adversarial samples into the visual input stream. Drawing upon established neural network vulnerabilities and the specific architectures of common learning methods utilized in this context, we successfully established that both the same-class and diverse adversarial samples can effectively manipulate the learned policies of these agents. Furthermore, while individual perturbations exhibit limited transferability across different models, aggregating multiple adversarial examples yields robust transferability. This work underscores the necessity of accounting for adversarial risks when assessing the robustness of reinforcement learning systems and develops a practical framework to quantify these vulnerabilities.

The corresponding non-conservative Schrödinger equation translates directly into the effective Dirac Hamiltonian, where NNN phases function as optical potentials within the lattice. The resulting 3+1 dimensional dynamics occur in the context of the generated effective Dirac Hamiltonian, with NNN phases serving as the generated light-matter coupling at the nodes of the lattice. This study investigates risk-sensitive reinforcement learning (RL) in non-stationary environments, a domain that remains under-explored. Since ensuring optimal long-term performance in such settings is challenging, a more realistic and viable approach is adopted. We propose learning algorithms that only require the user to specify a "variation budget"—an upper limit on the total number of significant parameter shifts over time. We provide a rigorous mathematical definition of these jumps and prove that there exists an upper bound on the cumulative regret experienced by these algorithmic strategies when they respect this budget constraint. Based on this bound, a primary algorithm is developed that is guaranteed to match the theoretical performance limits. Additionally, supporting algorithms are detailed to ensure cumulative regret scales sublinearly with time $t$ ($o(t)$) as long as the environment's parameter variations remain within the specified budget. Experimental results confirm that this risk-sensitive methodology significantly outperforms standard, risk-neutral approaches, particularly in tasks that demand careful risk management. Furthermore, these methods substantially reduce the variation budget requirement compared to existing risk-learning algorithms.

Organizations face escalating demands for new features, bug fixes, and improvements as their projects grow in complexity. To handle this demand, many employ issue tracking systems (ITS) to log tasks, manage work, and provide project insights through status and timing data. While past attempts have attempted to predict demand using textual comments or metadata found in issue requests, such methods often yield inconsistent results. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging the structural topology of request dependency graphs (RGs) to demand forecasting. Specifically, we analyze the network properties inherent in the way issues reference one another, under the premise that a task's information and context are distributed across its connected neighbors in an RG. Validated through a controlled field study, our findings reveal that demand related to priority, status updates, and completion times can be accurately projected using metrics like graph centrality. We have further developed practical algorithms to apply these prows effectively.

Distributed machine learning (DML) across time-varying networks is essential for numerous applications; however, existing virtual synchronization protocols often demand strict assumptions regarding communication latency bounds, network topology, or both, which limits their practicality in dynamic environments. This work introduces coordination methods that alleviate these rigid constraints for gradient-descent-based optimizers, enabling communication-free local updates regardless of message delays or varying topology. Under conditions of delayed exchanges, we derive bounds ensuring convergence to a $\delta$-neighborhood of the global optimum for strongly convex and convex objectives; our approach handles constant sampling intervals without requiring synchronization. Furthermore, adaptive sampling strategies are proposed that guarantee exact convergence for strongly convex functions with diminishing sample gaps and asymptotic convergence for convex functions with larger gaps, without necessitating network details such as topology or bounds on delays, delays, or varying topology.

This study introduces an on-chip multi-grating apparatus designed to generate and manipulate the optical lattices and single-species atoms, such as Rubidium. By leveraging a four-surface coupling technique that directs a single input waveguide photon, the device produces a 3D conical grating array that serves as an optical dipole trap for individual Rb atoms. This effective trapping mechanism supports resonances in driving Rb transitions using the same cones of light. Simultaneously, the setup grooms the waveguide field into cones to excite the atoms, triggering the atom-light interaction. Resonant excitations spur atoms to scatter photons, which are then collected by the coupling nanoparticle and conveyed back to the waveguide for detection. The entire system operates within a 200-nm spatial confinement, enabling ultra-compact, high-fidelity single-atom resonance fluorescence while fostering scalable, integrated platforms for ongoing quantum information processing.

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have proven highly effective for inverse design challenges, specifically in creating new chemical compounds with tailored properties. In this study, we employ ANNs to synthesize molecular structures featuring specific conformational properties by interacting with flexible multi-ring systems. Our approach utilizes ANNs to generate molecular graph representations, which are subsequently assessed through 3D molecular scoring functions engineered to capture conformational equilibrium without relying on the computationally expensive quantum mechanical calculations that limit current methods. This proposed framework effectively simulates the ground-state potential energy surfaces of the molecules' ground-state conformations.

Continuous-time dynamic optimization is frequently employed as a foundational model across engineering and economic fields. While numerical optimization methods must be resorted to when analytical solutions are unattainable, existing approaches often suffer from the "curse of dimensionality," imposing strict limits on problem complexity. This paper introduces a dimensionless-free numerical method rooted in deep reinforcement learning. By utilizing deep neural networks to efficiently and accurately solve the associated optimal control problem, the proposed framework offers significant computational efficiency.

A rational function $f$ defined over the extended complex plane $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ with precisely two critical points is classified as bicritical. By leveraging the theory of normalizations for these functions, we establish that the set of all map parameters can be partitioned into finitely families. This classification enables a direct comparison with known results regarding the parameter spaces of complex one-dimensional holomorphic endomorphisms of degree $d$.

We examine the sample efficiency required to localize and perform local estimation within a sparse high-dimensional linear framework, targeting unknown parameters that are only approximately "0-\subgaussian." Our approach introduces adaptive empirical priors, initially centered around a data-driven estimate of the precision matrix and tuned by the problem's minimax radius of sparsity. Under this prior distribution, marginalizing out the high-dimensional coefficients yields an approximate Bayesian linear model that can be solved efficiently. Notably, the empirical priors we propose belong to a broader class of adaptive tools capable of delivering sparse posterior distributions that remain close in $\ell_2$-norm to the true ground truth. When integrated into the empirical prior scheme, the resulting posterior samples—specifically the near-optimal minimal sparsity solutions—achieve the same location precision as the true parameters.

Power consumption is a critical factor in manufacturing, as it directly influences production costs and environmental sustainability. While the influence of machine parameters on power usage has been examined in literature regarding turning, milling, and drilling, the specific impacts of these parameters are often evaluated individually, ignoring their potential interactions. This study addresses that gap by analyzing the combined machine parameter impacts on power consumption during drilling using the Response Surface Methodology with a Central Composite Design. Drawing from previous knowledge of optimal parameters, the authors designed an experiment to minimize drilling energy use. The resulting models for each parameter and their interactions were validated through an analysis of variance. Ultimately, benchmarking these findings against current industry standards demonstrated that accounting for parameter interactions effectively Distinguished the optimal machine settings, successfully reducing power consumption by approximately 5.5% compared to conventional practices.

The exponent d_s characterizes how the volume of spheres evolves over time in a diffusion process. The asymptotic count of subgraphs with self-avoiding walks (ASAWs) depends on this dimension. The authors derive an asymptotic formula for ATWAS with low degrees where d_s exceeds a calculable threshold determined by the graph's ATWAS dimension. The authors calculate d_s for d-skeletal structures and generalize the formula to arbitrary degrees with ATWAS-convergent limits. The formula's accuracy is verified against simulations and computations for d-skeletal and other graph types with known limits. The authors extend the formula's applicability beyond d-skeletal structures to graphs with empirically determined ATWAS-convergent limits.

By analyzing data from the BESIII experiment corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 1.77 fb$^{-1}$, this study investigates the decay properties of J/$\psi$ into B$_{c}^{+}$B$_{c}^{-}$. The cross section for this gamma-fission-induced transition was determined to be 5.8$^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ pb. Furthermore, a pronounced peak was detected at the center-of-mass energy of 4.230 GeV in the B$_{c}^{+}$B$_{c}^{-}$ invariant mass spectrum. This feature, labeled as the $Y(4230)$ resonance, exhibits the same characteristics as those previously documented in e$^{+}$e$^{-}$ annihilation processes. Leveraging recent theoretical frameworks, this work proposes interpreting the $Y(4230)$ as a charmonium state designated as 4S.

This study introduces a metric for assessing the quality of collected online signature templates, acknowledging that templates vary in standard. The authors propose and evaluate three complementary measures to effectively characterize templates: (1) the ratio of distinct signatures to the total number of samples, (2) the overlap between consecutive signature instances, and (3) the similarity between a sliding window of consecutive instances and the entire dataset.

We examine a dopant moving within the magnetic insulator La$_2$Ti$_2$O$_5$Nb, a material believed to possess a half-integer spin per cell that forms a spin liquid supported by strong quantum and geometric frustration. Due to this high degree of frustration, the dopant encounters significant quantum resistance when entering or exiting a site, yielding an effective spin of zero or one/2 depending on the specific configuration. Consequently, we have developed an effective model for this quantum tunneling process and derived a formula for magnetic dressing as a function of the dopant's momentum. Our findings reveal that while the dopant behaves as a heavy particle with negligible free movement, its magnetic dressing exhibits substantial momentum dependence. This observed variation offers a novel perspective on how to interpret the movement of defects within frustrated quantum systems.

This work extends that work by exploring how rotation enhances N enrichment in massive stars and enriches secondary N in AGB stars. Defined as the blending of two or more languages within a single conversation, code-switching (CS) is a widespread global phenomenon. This study introduces the inaugural comprehensive multilingual CS dataset, the Chinese-English Bilingual Conversational Encoding-Decoding Challenge (CED-Ch-En) codec-switching corpus, consisting of 135,000 CS sentences paired with their non-Switching equivalents. We also establish several benchmarks utilizing CS speech samples across four languages—Chinese, English, Hindi, Spanish, and Portuguese—as well as encoded data in those same linguistic pairs for testing purposes. These materials are intended to facilitate deeper investigation into the effects of code-switching on machine translation systems and cross-lingual speech technologies.

Biomedical graphs are increasingly essential for modeling intricate interactions within living systems, and recent breakthroughs in representation learning have significantly transformed machine learning applications within this field. This review examines past progress and emerging opportunities in using graph-based learning for the life sciences, beginning with an overview of various graph types employed in these contexts. It examines recent achievements in representing graph-structured genomic and proteomic data, followed by models of biological entities and processes such as tissue and organ systems. The discussion extends to clinical data, including electronic health records and patterns associated with diseases. Finally, we explore emerging methodologies and novel avenues for future research in the domain of biomedicine.

White dwarfs are expected to brighten gradually due to energy released by core-collapsing Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) as they annihilate. Current observations of certain white dwarfs, which show surface luminosity exceeding theoretical cooling predictions for their age, may provide evidence for this phenomenon, thereby constraining the parameter space of WIMPs. In this study, I refine existing cooling models by accounting for ongoing central-temperature gradients caused by both accretion and WIMP annihilation, utilizing an analytical polytropic structure to model these effects. My calculations indicate that for most viable WIMP models, the resulting luminosity contribution is negligible compared to standard cooling rates, although early-phase accretion can significantly enhance WIMP-induced light output if a system retains heavy elements on its surface. Specifically, a sustained surface accretion rate of approximately $10^{-10} M_{\odot} \, \mathrm{Gyr}^{-1}$ could produce measurable anomalous luminosity even for the most particle-interaction-favored parameter regions. To effectively constrain such scenarios, future studies must identify systems with ages exceeding 10 Gyr that exhibit heavy surface-element enrichment.

Many individuals underestimate the privacy risks associated with uploading photos to the internet, often failing to recognize how easily personal details can be extracted from them. This paper introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor (GPA), a user-friendly browser application that analyzes a selected image to identify potentially sensitive information and assess overall privacy. The ADV user interface guides individuals through enhancing an image's security by addressing detected issues. GPA determines the confidence level of discovered data by evaluating the presence or absence of landmarks, outdoor scenes, readable text, and specific objects. Additionally, it calculates the image's resolution impact on data precision. The application employs the OpenCV and Google Lens APIs to recognize content while establishing a knowledge graph linked to DBpedia for data association. Following the extraction of data and their connections, GPA appraises privacy by estimating the likelihood that any included entity is personally identifiable.

This passage outlines a mathematical framework for radiation using probability measures on a local connection of the principal unitary bundle associated with the particle's mass-shell in Minkowski spacetime. Adopting a first-order formalism, the model incorporates retarded interactions, implying that a particle continuously interacts with its own history. Consequently, formal mechanisms for radiative mass and momentum transfer occur dynamically between the particle and its trail. The authors demonstrate that, within this framework, asymptotic states exist in relation to the electromagnetic field; by applying the S-matrix to these states, they successfully validate standard low-energy Breit-Wheeler formulas for scattering.

Solar atmospheric observations reveal magnetic fields and intense heat within the corona, the mechanisms of which remain unclear. Nansoflares—microscopic, brief bursts of radiation and heat generated between magnetic field lines—may explain these features. Although our current understanding of their nature and function relies on both theory and observation, more research is needed to clarify how they shape coronal dynamics and energy balance, particularly as high-resolution imaging from the Solar Orbiter (2020) offers new data to investigate these questions through direct observation of nanoflare events and their effects on the corona.

Social influence prediction is a critical challenge in graph analytics, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as a promising approach. Although GNNs often lack the sample efficiency required for practical applications—necessity large datasets that are often unavailable in real-world scenarios—this paper addresses this limitation by proposing the use of data augmentation for social influence prediction. Specifically, we introduce a novel augmentation technique called influence perturbation, designed to maintain the integrity of influence relationships within social networks. This method supports both generative adversarial network (GNNs) and link reconstruction models. Comprehensive experiments conducted across six real-world datasets, including those with missing influence data, demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances GNN performance for predicting influence in social networks.

Defining quantum field theory complexity is challenging because it lacks a standard definition and a clear operator basis. This paper concentrates on conformal field theories within 1+1 dimensions, utilizing the holographic dictionary to draw insights from matrix models like the Kitaev model and SYK models. It posits that for such CFTs, complexity arises from iterating simple local operators to construct more complex ones, with the number of required iterations determined by their distance from the boundary on the conformal light cone. supported by an operator expansion, this framework yields a specific formula for computing operator complexity, highlighting a strong alignment with the Holographic Complexity conjecture. The workhypothesizes that the Holographic Complexity conjecture holds true for an extensive range of theories beyond those explicitly tested so far.

This research addresses pose estimation using a single lensless image, where the objective is to determine the object's three-dimensional position from its microshadow cast on a micromachined diffuser. We evaluate Fisher Information Matrix-derived estimates for the lower bound of localization error, comparing them against standard optimization strategies as well as closed-form solutions. Results indicate that the closed-form approach achieves initial performance closer to the Cramér-Rao lower bound; however, from a specific signal-to-noise ratio threshold onward, optimization methods surpass it, producing higher estimation accuracy and proving more robust.

Various models rooted in string theory feature hidden sectors that offer significant cosmological and particle physics implications, including dark matter, mass hierarchy explanations, and solutions to the \textit{muon} anomaly, alongside the mechanism for electroweak symmetry breaking. This paper explores how visible and hidden sectors might connect through a composite mechanism arising from extra dimensions of spacelike character. Specifically, fermions occupy these extra dimensions as spacelike geodesics, whereas gauge bosons emerge as the non-linear gauge symmetries inherent to those metrics. Consequently, dark matter candidates, neutrinos, and Higgs bosons reside within the hidden sector alongside dark radiation. In this framework, dark matter and the dark thermal bath interact solely via sectors other than the standard model, while neutrinos and the Higgs interact with hot plasma exclusively through weak forces. We demonstrate that this setup yields an improved fit to experimental data regarding the expansion history of the universe compared to the $\Lambda$CDM model, including a refined description of ${{}^{21}}$ cm line anomalies and the large-scale structure of the universe. Additionally, the predicted spectrum of primordial gravitational waves is found to be significantly suppressed.

This paper details the measurement of same-sign W boson pair ($WW$) production through proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, utilizing 40 fb$^{-1}$ of data collected by the CMS detector at the LHC. The analysis proceeds via the all-lepton ($\ell=e,\mu$) and $\ell\nu$ decay channels for the W bosons. An observable cross section of 109 $\pm$ 13 (statistical) $\pm$ 13 (systematic) fb is derived for events with at least two electrons or muons of identical charge, while a higher cross section of 109 $\pm$ 13 (statistical) $\pm$ 13 (systematic) fb is obtained for events with exactly two electrons or muons after applying specific event topology requirements. These findings align well with Standard Model predictions.

This paper proposes the CoDCam framework, a machine learning system designed to train models for cameras with both a monochrome sensor (capable solely of capturing intensity but offering a 20% width advantage over RGB) and an RGB color sensor. By leveraging the wider field of view from the monochrome channel and the color data from the RGB channel, the single model jointly predicts monochrome color images and a corresponding error map that highlights areas of chromatic discrepancy between the two inputs. Validated on a new dataset of paired images captured by these dual cameras, the study demonstrates that this joint learning approach surpasses traditional single-mode models in predictive accuracy. Additional applications include generating confidence masks to indicate specific discoloration and facilitating the development of hybrid post-processing algorithms.

We investigate the lensing consistency parameter, $A_L$, within extended $\Lambda$CDM frameworks utilizing CMB data from the Planck 2018 DR2 release. Leveraging low-frequency template (LFI) observations from the Planck satellite alone, and subsequently in combination with external datasets including ACT, SPT, and BICEP2/Keck, we assess the performance of the low-resolution template power spectrum alongside higher-resolution contributions from the latter two experiments. Our analysis demonstrates that incorporating SPT and the SPT+ACT combined dataset yields the most significant improvement in constraining $A_L$. Specifically, combining SPT with ACT results in a $1.7\,\sigma$ preference for the canonical $\Lambda$CDM value of $A_L=1$. Furthermore, we explore the interplay between the low-$A_L$ preference derived from SPT/ACT and the low-$A_L$ tendency suggested by the tension in the CMB angular power spectrum at small scales ($\ell \lesssim 2000$).

Over the counter, over time, software systems accumulate technical debt that diminishes their maintainability. To tackle this challenge, researchers have developed various automated techniques, such as those capable of generating remediation plans or even executing them directly. A central but complex aspect of automating these interventions is understanding their potential ripple effects: when one issue is fixed, numerous other issues may emerge or resolve themselves. While existing approaches often model these dependencies using static dependency graphs, this approach offers limited capacity for representing dynamic behaviors. To address this limitation, the authors introduce the concept of "meta-maintenance" to track how maintenance activities influence software systems over time and spaces. The proposed formal model utilizes an LTS (labeled transition system), enabling the automated derivation of maintenance chains—consequences that may involve both positive outcomes and negative side effects. Furthermore, the techniques allow for the identification of potential conflicts within these maintenance interventions and enable the prediction of their overall impact.

We report the results of a high-resolution spectroscopic study of BD And, a variable binary star located in Andromeda. The system's position within the W UMa contact binary sequence on both the orbital period and effec-tive temperature (T<sub>eff</sub>) scales suggests it belongs to the group of long-period U-type contact binaries. Our analysis reveals that the main (primary) component exhibits spectral signatures of G-type stars with rotation velocities (V sin i) between 10 and 20 km s<sup>-1</sup>. Given BD And's location in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, the primary star is likely either a slightly evolved main-sequence star or a main-sequence star that has not yet reached zero-age. The companion is a weak M-dwarf. Our findings regarding the primary star's characteristics and the system's behavior align with predictions from evolutionary models. Additionally, our derived radial velocity semi-amplitudes for the system are K<sub>1</sub> = 105.7 ± 0.3 km s<sup>-1</sup> and K<sub>2</sub> = 38.1 ± 0.3 km s<sup>-1</sup>.

This study extends research previously undertaken in collaboration with the second author and P. Daskalopoulos. That earlier collaboration, conducted alongside J.L. V\'{a}zquez, introduced the fractionable Yamabe flow relevant to fractional curvature and established existence theorems for mild (semi-group) solutions. The current article advances this research by demonstrating that for a specific set of data, the flow exhibits convergence within a broader framework. Our methodology draws heavy inspiration from the significant contributions of C. Safferman.

Cross-domain recommendation aims to enhance suggestions by leveraging auxiliary information from related domains. Yet, existing multi-domain approaches often rely heavily on the assumption that domain pairs are fully connected, causing information from distant domains to introduce unnecessary noise. Furthermore, current methods typically perform global information aggregation, which ignores the fact that only a limited amount of external data is truly helpful in these tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce MSDCR (Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation), a novel framework designed to facilitate flexible cross-domain learning. MSDCR achieves this through two core mechanisms: Multi-Domain Routing (MDR) and Sparse Domain Collaborative Embedding (SDCE). The MDR module learns the structural relationships between domains to establish a dynamic routing path for accessing external data, effectively linking each domain with others it is most relevant to. Consequently, the SDCE module acquires key representations from these selected partners via a hybrid process combining self-, mutual, and cross-domain attention. Evaluations on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MSDCR significantly outperforms existing baseline models as well as other advanced techniques specifically designed for multi-dense or sparse environments.

We establish that for any smooth projective scheme, the vector space capturing the first-order variations of a sheaf equipped with either an orthogonal (respectively symplectic) structure corresponds exactly to the first hyper-cohomology of a specific, related complex inside that sheaf. Additionally, we present the deformation theory for these structures sheathed on complex surfaces, utilizing a specific result regarding the exact sequence associated with orthogonal sheaves on complex projectic varieties.

We examine approximating an unknown function $f$ within the unit ball of the Reynolds range of operators of the form $\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}_\alpha \circ \mathcal{F}_\mathcal{H}$, where $\mathcal{A}_\alpha$ is a smoothing operator and the composition is trained using $n$ noisy data points. This approach, which includes models like deep neural networks and regularized neural operators, is analyzed by viewing it as an approximation strategy under data constraints. Our findings reveal a trade-off between estimation error and the size of the target approximation space: as the dimensions of this space (specifically the smoothing parameter $\alpha$) increase, the required sample size $n$ must also grow to guarantee accuracy. We provide explicit complexity estimates for Sobolev-type target classes and show that these results closely match current optimal rates. Additionally, we establish that our method enjoys robust generalization, recovering $f$ even when data is severely corrupted, with the recovered function approaching any non-smooth $f$ as long as it lies within the unit ball of $\mathcal{A}_\alpha$.

We have developed a kinetic framework to simulate the cooling and expansion of a two-flavor parton system, utilizing simplified scattering cross-sections. By incorporating both mass and flavor structures into the kinematics of these collisions, the model effectively simulates parton-system dynamics during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. We have then used this simulation to calculate transport parameters—specifically the shear viscosity to density ratio and binary collision cross-sections—required to reproduce experimental data from the SnN model for these processes.

Local magnetic moments form with high probability in insulating systems that feature disordered electronic landscapes, specifically falling within the random singlet phase, which is characterized by exponentially decaying spin correlations at long distances. These spin interactions drive the dynamic critical exponent toward large values and push the system's relaxation behavior into a very slow regime, typically following a $t^{-1/2}$ law. Despite this prediction, experimental observations and numerical simulations often reveal significantly slower dynamics, sometimes approaching logarithmic time dependence. In this study, we present theoretical evidence that identifies the origin of such anomalous dynamics: the presence of weakly bound states situated just beneath the Fermi level. By employing an exact derivation of localized bound-state probabilities and incorporating a perturbative treatment of these states' impacts on dynamics, we demonstrate that they account for this unusually sluggish relaxation behavior. Furthermore, we propose experimental methods to distinguish between the standard critical dynamics and this new mechanism of anomalous relaxation.

The Orbit Generating System (OGS) for a group $G$ is defined as the most compact collection of group elements from which every other element in $G$ can be derived using only the group operation. In this article, we introduce a method to determine the unique OGS in both additive and multiplicative non-abelian groups, demonstrated here with specific reference to the general linear group $GL(n, \mathbb{F}_q)$. The unique OGS established within a group is termed "canonical," as it remains invariant across all group isomorphisms. Furthermore, given any set of elements belonging to the group, we outline an algorithm designed to identify the nearest element to the canonical OGS.

"This work presents an approach to linearized perturbations of scalar field theory featuring two interacting fields, specifically targeting kink solitons arising from the potential described by Eq. (2.1). Initially, we demonstrate that solving the eigenvalue problem for the associated time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation (Eq. 3.4) is equivalent to solving the underlying Sturm-Liouville problem (Eq. 3.5). Based on this equivalence, we derive the complete set of eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions. subsequently, utilizing these spectral solutions, we construct the explicit time-dependent modes for both the field perturbations and their conjugate momenta. Finally, we utilize this complete mode basis to formulate the back-reaction on the background kink induced by quantum fluctuations."

Current robot learning-from-demonstration frameworks frequently rely on inverse reinforcement learning (IRL), which often struggles with the computational expense of evaluating all possible policies during training. Although recent advances have mitigated this by incorporating prior knowledge, they still fail to distinguish between useful and detrimental observations. Nuisance events, like a person accidentally knocking over a cup while guiding a robot, can mislead standard IRL by suggesting poor policies. We introduce NUIL (Nuisance Observations Handling via Maximum Likelihood), a new algorithm that actively filters out noise. By integrating a probabilistic model of the supervisor's behavior, NUIL identifies and suppresses noise, yielding more reliable reward functions. Distinct from prior work filtering out pure outliers, our method robustly handles corrupted data where observations are slightly distorted. Experimental validation on two real-world robotic tasks confirms its efficacy.

Let $H$ denote a subgroup within the fundamental group $\pi_1(X)$ of a geodesic metric space $X$. We establish that if the space $X/H$ satisfies the Strong H-SLT condition with respect to $\pi_1(X)$, then there exists at least one covering map from $X$ to $X$ that induces an isomorphism on the quotient by $H$ in the fundamental group.

We propose a two-phase algorithm designed to present optimal or near-optimal control solutions for highly complex systems, specifically focusing on model formulation and optimal determination. The first phase focuses on addressing model formulation challenges, particularly for nonlinear magnetic systems with limited prior knowledge, by leveraging a data-driven nonlinear model identification method that utilizes a bank of excitations to enable parallel identification of multiple models. Subsequently, the second phase addresses determining the best control trajectory across these various models through optimization techniques. It uses a multi-objective decision-making framework to select the optimal solution based on results from diverse models. Notably, this second phase also determines control parameters for the inferior models within each solution. The validity of this approach was demonstrated using a physical example involving magnetic actuators for contact force regulation, confirming that considering multiple models yields a single optimal control solution.

We examine the role of gas dynamical friction in driving orbital decay and triggering gas accretion onto supermassive black holes (BHs) within high-redshift star-forming galaxies. Utilizing cosmological simulations, we simulate smooth gaseous disks and incorporate massive bodies representing both BHs and stellar clusters. Our results show that orbital energy loss from dynamical friction causes these simulated BHs to sink to the common potential minimum, where they merge. Our simulations indicate that dynamical friction can drive significant gas inflows, generating black hole (BH) masses of $10^8$ to $10^9$ M$\odot$ within 1 Gyr. These findings suggest that a central BH with a mass of $10^6$ M$\odot$ can grow to $10^8$ M$\odot$ in a smooth gaseous disk through this mechanism. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a dispersed stellar core also experiences orbital decay due to dynamical friction, reaching the center of the galaxy and inducing gas inflows that generate a central BH of $10^8$ to $10^9$ M$\odot$ in 1 Gyr. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have proven highly effective for extracting information from data in large-scale experiments, such as those conducted in particle physics and astronomy. Despite these successes, common obstacles like overfitting, underfitting, and model selection bias often complicate their application. This paper proposes a strategy to alleviate or eliminate underfitting, overfitting, and selection bias by randomly shuffling input data across different scales before feeding it into the network. We validate the efficacy of this approach through simulations involving the Higgs boson decay into four-lepton final states.

Preprint servers have become essential components of academic research infrastructure, allowing researchers to share their work prior to formal journal publication. Over the last three decades, the number of such servers expanded exponentially, yet preprints constitute only a small fraction—less than 5%—of total research articles. This study offers a refined analysis by examining 15 years of data (2005–2019) to assess publication rates across various disciplines. We focus our examination of subject-specific trends on a limited set of preprint servers with archived data for this period, analyzing 155,209 papers drawn from 11 major journals. Our findings indicate that adoption of preprints varies significantly by field, with life sciences showing substantially higher uptake than physics or computer science. Furthermore, we observed that articles featuring authors who submitted their work to life science preprint services had a significantly shorter time to publication compared to those without such submissions.

Robust research infrastructure is essential for the rigorous, reproducible conduct of scholarship, particularly in fields increasingly reliant on data and complex processes. While open-source tools can substantially lower barriers to accessing this infrastructure, the setup and maintenance of such environments demand time and expertise that many researchers lack. We introduce the *CReditive* Python package to bridge this skills gap by standardizing the reproduction of the statistical analysis underlying our own research. Beyond serving as a reusable research log for experimental procedures and data handling, *CReditive* acts as an adaptable template for new studies, thereby facilitating scientific progress. By treating research analysis as modular "functions," the tool enables easy adaptation to different research contexts while simultaneously documenting research infrastructure as transferable "functions." Consequently, a researcher's iterative development process effectively transforms into a living document of their research methods, or "research codebook."

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent a class of materials defined by multiple principal metallic elements, renowned for their exceptional mechanical properties and versatile applications. The utilization of machine learning (ML) has recently proven valuable in examining and developing these alloys, delivering swift predictions of material characteristics with forecasting accuracy that frequently matches experimental data. Nevertheless, significant hurdles remain in the field, including limited generalizability outside tested scenarios and the labor-intensive nature of acquiring high-quality data. Emerging ML strategies are now being employed to overcome these obstacles specifically within the context of HEAs; this review explores current applications and introduces novel methodologies for designing, training, and leveraging such models for ground-breaking results and innovative ideas. Furthermore, the paper outlines the various computational tools required to execute this work and emphasizes the critical role of domain expertise in effectively using them.

Probabilistic frameworks are fundamental to machine learning, yet they are underutilized in natural language processing (NLP). This underexploitation stems from the difficulty in state estimation; that is, inferring latent variables from observable data. Advances in variational inference have addressed this challenge by reformulating state estimation as a constrained optimization problem, leveraging efficient, gradient-based solvers. We adapt these methodologies for probabilistic modeling in language and introduce a new algorithm for latent-variable NLP. Our contribution includes a general framework for probabilistic language modeling and a specific model built upon latent Dirichlet allocation. Extensive experiments on extensive datasets demonstrate that the proposed algorithms and models outperform non-inferior baselines, often achieving superior results.

Binary matrix sampling is essential across many scientific domains, including reverse ecology for microbial communities and binary matrix factorization. Traditional methods draw samples via uniform or constrained distributions using algorithms like swapping, although achieving exact distributional samples often requires impractical time. This study introduces a novel, rapid swapping algorithm designed to generate exact samples under the product-partition distribution. It leverages a product decomposition of the product-partition distribution specific to binary matrices, adopting a randomized, local, and guided approach informed by initial independent draws. This work examines the dynamics of rigid water dimers simulated using event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) methods. Specifically, we focus on the global orientational relaxation over extended timescales and compare these findings with results from local reversible Metropolis algorithms. A key motivation for this comparison is that the widely used reversible algorithm suffers from significant slow-down in relaxation due to its local nature, an issue ECMС aims to mitigate through superior long-time exploration. To achieve rigorous local reversibility, our ECMС implementation utilizes an infinite chain configuration. Through analysis of time correlation functions, we demonstrate that even with an infinite chain, ECMC exhibits comparable slow relaxation behavior to the reversible algorithm at very long times, a result consistent with recent theoretical predictions. Nevertheless, we establish that ECMC remains significantly more effective than the Metropolis algorithm for sampling long-timescales, achieving approximately a 100-fold speed-up in relaxation rates while maintaining excellent configurational sampling. Furthermore, we investigate the effects of numerical finite precision on the algorithms and assess how variations in ECMC control parameters influence the relaxation process.

Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) involves identifying audio sources and estimating their directional angles using microphone arrays. While recent advancements in machine learning have significantly boosted performance, these deep models often lack interpretability, making it difficult to pinpoint specific failure modes. Specifically, we integrate a convolutional recurrent neural network with a quantization model composed of two convolutions and two pooling layers to construct a two-class Bayesian support vector machine framework. This approach enables robust feature extraction through convolutions, temporal modeling via recurrence, and theoretically sound classification using the Bayesian SVM. Experimental results demonstrate improved robustness to background noise and the novelty of our method in applying this combination specifically to sound detection and localization.

Recent technological strides have made wireless communication more popular than ever, enabling a diverse range of applications from virtual reality and autonomous driving to mobile health monitoring. This work examines local synchronization patterns within a network of more than 2000 phase oscillators, each governed by unique dynamics and coupling parameters. This study presents an analysis of ground states and excited states in helium-like systems confined within Reimann's atom chip, focusing on the interplay between correlation effects and confinement strength. These VMC calculations demonstrate clear improvements over the Heitler-Damgaard (HS) approximation, with the magnitude of gain depending on the system and confinement parameters. Lastly, high-precision fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo (FN-DMC) results are presented to serve as robust benchmarks for various computational methods.

The dynamics of wide binary systems offer a unique opportunity to validate laws of gravity in the extremely low gravitational fields found at the edges of galaxies, where General Relativity predicts deviations. By leveraging modern astrometric data from the Gaia mission, researchers have significantly expanded catalogues of wide binaries, enabling a more rigorous statistical examination of gravity under these specific low-acceleration conditions. By modeling the orbital dynamics of these stars, the researchers place new, tighter constraints on the parameter $\beta$ (used in modified gravity theories), limiting it to values less than $1.9 \times 10^{-2}$ with 95% confidence. These stringent limits on $\beta$ are derived independently from previous studies that analyzed the same dataset, confirming the robustness of the wide binary test for alternative gravity models.

Cross-correlation analysis serves as a potent instrument for exploring the mutual dynamics between financial time series representing the same underlying assets but across different dimensions. This study offers a novel methodology to group Indian stock market series based on such correlations. Through this approach, we reveal the complex inter-series relationships that series grouping methods often obscure. The proposed technique introduces an innovative series classification framework grounded in cross-analysis, leveraging these series groups subsequently as distinct input features for standard financial forecasting models.

Terahertz radiation enables the selective tuning of vibrations within molecules and crystal lattices, revealing how the circular paths taken by ions generate inertial influences on electrons that parallel the classical concepts of Coriolis and centrifugal forces. These forces arise from both direct coupling and indirect mechanisms, the latter driven by the deformation of electronic charge distributions in response to THz-driven molecular or lattice oscillations. Consequently, this phenomenon offers a pathway to probe intricate quantum phenomena, including superconductivity and the Hall effect, through experiments utilizing Terahertz-pulse spectroscopy and control techniques.

Clique-Through Rate (CTR) prediction is vital for advertising systems, yet it is constrained by the scarcity of positive samples for newly launched ads, resulting in subpar predictions. This paper proposes a new dual-tower CTR model that integrates contrastive learning to leverage extensive, loosely labeled data for improving performance on novel advertisements. In the dual-tayer structure, user and advertisement features are extracted independently; furthermore, contrastive learning is employed to align the representation of user-ad pairs with the individual features of users and ads separately. Extensive experiments conducted on two real-world datasets confirm that incorporating contrastive learning substantially boosts CTR prediction accuracy, particularly for ads with limited click data.

Business processes encompass both structured sequences and semi-structured variations. However, knowledge-intensive processes (KIBP) interact complexly with their environment, encompassing external systems, humans, and intricate data flows. Due to this complexity, KIHP cannot be fully represented as standard structured business processes. Instead, they require specific modeling techniques capable of handling uncertainty and varying execution paths. Process patterns offer a solution by providing reusable components that define specific challenges and opportunities within these workflows, serving as building blocks for management. This research introduces a methodology that leverages pattern-based modeling techniques for KIHP while exploring their integration with existing KIHP. Furthermore, we examine how patterns interact with other processes, environmental factors, and people to reflect real-world interactions. Ultimately, our approach facilitates the modeling of complex processes and supports their effective analysis and understanding.

Wildfire atmospheric plumes are massive sources of aerosols that negatively impact air quality, solar energy output, and aviation safety. This study analyzes satellite data from the OMI instrument aboard the NASA Earth Observing System satellite to assess atmospheric SO2 concentrations following the 2019 Australian bushfires. By examining the fires' sulfur emissions and tracking the resulting pollutant cloud as it moved across the continent and into the Indian Ocean, we mapped their spatial and temporal evolution. These atmospheric analyses are supported by ground-based spectral data from the Total Column Spectrometer (TDCS) network in Australia, which helped contextualize the OMI findings and provide complementary observations of the sulfur dioxide columns.

Offering meaningful privacy protection for users of location-based systems is exceptionally difficult, particularly when multiple positions within short intervals are exposed. Current anonymization methods, which typically limit differential privacy leakage to only the most recent position, often fail to provide adequate safeguarding in these scenarios. This work addresses the first stage of an anonymization framework tailored for differential privacy that considerspositional trajectories. We examine the single-dimensional continuous-time movement of an entity and determine the optimal amount of privacy noise required to ensure a desired level of differential privacy between any two adjacent locations. Our contributions include contributions to multiple positional data contexts: we analyze how noise requirements scale with the frequency of location tracking, extend our findings to two-dimensional spaces, and generalize these results to scenarios involving a cohort of users.

Multisite investigations utilizing resting-state fMRI have grown substantially in recent years. Nevertheless, fundamental inquiries regarding optimal data management, harmonization protocols, and the validity of inferential statistics across and within fMRI centers remain unresolved. This study examined inter-site differences by analyzing data from 108 typically developing children (ages 7–12) collected at three institutions. We evaluated three analytical strategies: (1) pooling all data into a combined dataset, (2) conducting separate scans-per-site analyses while pooling final F-maps, and (3- performing fully decentralized site-specific inference. Using canonical network activation as a benchmark, we measured detection power for inter-group comparisons and assessed effect-size estimation accuracy via bias. Results indicated that the power to distinguish genuine effects did not vary significantly between the first two approaches. In contrast, the third method suffered from reduced power, likely due to inflated error rates from aggregating site-specific F-maps. Regarding bias in effect-size measurement, the power-based combination of F-maps introduced slight underestimates, while the fully separate analysis caused substantial underestimation. These findings support the conclusion that, for typical development fMRI studies, there is no clear power advantage in pooling raw data versus pooling F-maps; however, the latter approach is preferable for studies involving multiple sites as it minimizes bias.
