A strategy to enhance entanglement within cavity magnomechanical systems is introduced, involving the sequential interaction of two magnon-cavity-mechanoscators with a succession of single photons. Initially, we examine the entanglement properties of two bonds formed between a cavity-mechanoscillator pair and between a two-level system and a resonator, each composed of one N-level atom interacting with either a resonator or a combination of magnetostatic and mechanical elements. Subsequently, we propose a photon-mediated protocol to generate entanglement between two distinct N-level atom-cavity-mechanoscillator assemblies or between a pair of mechanical oscillators. Finally, we detail a parallel photon-based approach capable of generating Greenberger-Horne-Zeinberger-dihn (GHZ) states for multiple cavities, resonators, or pairs formed by two mechanical oscillators and two two-level atoms.

The one-loop triple-collinear operators concerning color and spin-space splittings across four processes (e.g., $q \to g \to q\bar{q}$, $g \to g \to q\bar{q}$, $q \to g \to q\bar{q}$) are derived. These are combined with corresponding two-collinear projections to form splitting matrices essential for constructing the NNLO-pp $\to$ jet+X matrix element. These results support the factorization of multi-jet components in antenna-based NNLO simulations, a capability already verified for single and double collinear limits. Single-splitting data align perfectly with known NNLO single-drop annihilation results, while double-splitting expressions have been cross-validated against known double-real emission terms for four-jet production.

"An implementation for one-dimensional local rings and an algorithmic proof of general resolution of singularities in singular are provided. Additionally, the paper features a generalization of Greenstein approximation Theorem specifically tailored for one-dimensional rings."

The sun's movement was pivotal in classical Islamic civilisation, particularly for determining prayer times and the start and end of the fast during Ramadan. While the 15th century saw numerous reports of fasts beginning and prayer routines commencing, these rituals varied by locality yet remained synchronized across vast geographic regions. This practice aligned with civil law mandates requiring synchronization. Nevertheless, the legal texts offer scarce details on the precise mechanisms used to achieve this coordination. This paper examines historical sources to explore how knowledge of the sun's position was applied to produce astronomical data and determine the daily horizons of solar rise and set. The study also addresses how this astronomical literacy facilitated the communication of sky events, notably the appearance of the moon crescent new to various communities.

This investigation examines a D2D system where a D2D pair enhances its link by deploying a deployed an IRS. The optimal numbers of active elements for both the D2D transmission/reception and the I RS are determined to maximize the sum spectral. efficiency. Due to the high complexity of the joint optimization problem, a decentralized solution utilizing a fixed-point-generative-iterative method is proposed. The convergence. properties. of this algorithm. are. also. analyzed. Moreover,. simulation. results. confirm. that the suggested approach. not. only. ensures. fast. convergence. but. also. outperforms. traditional. schemes.

Driven by the need to map responses to spatially varying stimuli within confined areas, the authors introduce an efficient version of 2D Laser Doppler Vibrometry capable of speeding up both the physical experiments and the subsequent data analysis. The proposed technique employs a 2D spatial light modulator to pre-pattern the illumination excitation, enabling simultaneous acquisition of phase and magnitude information by integrating this method with principal component analysis. Validation through simulations and experimental tests, specifically involving heated structures, demonstrates the technique's accuracy.

This paper investigates the spectral properties of first-order logic sentences within the context of finite structures, focusing on sentences involving up to four variables and binary predicates. While previous research by Holm, Rot, and Virag demonstrated that spectra for unsatisfactory or fully relational satisforable sentences with multiple variables and predicates are equivalent to those derived from monadic first-order logic on arbitrary structures, this work extends that inquiry by introducing a single symmetric binary relation to these formulas. Our primary finding reveals that, for at least three variables, using a single symmetric binary relation significantly increases the spectral expressive power of first-order logic when applied to finite structures.

This study investigates the viability of programmable electrostatic phase plates (pEPPs) as a tool for spherical aberration correction in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs), aiming to achieve sub-100 mnm spatial resolution. The proposed approach involves superimposing a phase gradient created by a programmable electric field with the natural lens of a simplified, uncorrected spherical-abstracted phase object. By pEPP-induced spherical aberration for specific coefficients, the system's wavefront is flattened, achieving near-optimal performance. Results indicate that pEPP can lower the probe Full-Half-Height (FFHW) to approximately 0.6 times that achievable with an equivalent static corrector while utilizing only natural lenses, generating field angles around 15 mrad. This achieves a target spatial resolution of approximately 9 nm. However, the method is constrained by limitations in generating extreme gradients and sustaining high fields; these constraints currently restrict the FFHW to about 3.5 MeV, though advancements in chip capabilities suggest that fully optimized systems using pEPPs will soon rival those equipped with traditional static correctors.

Guided by foundational concepts from Turing and Landauer, this paper constructs a framework where physical limits determine computability and complexity. We re-express classic results within this new formalism and define an expanded, dynamics-driven version of the Feynman path integral, which serves as an algorithm for solving the quantum mechanical Schrödinger equation. This innovation enables the evaluation of quantum anomalies, a previously unaddressed aspect of the path integral, offering both a simplified derivation of known anomalies and the ability to compute anomalies for new theories.

This paper presents a generalized formula for determining the number of unique location patterns in an n-step, d-dimensional space where movement is restricted to unit steps on coordinate axes (specifically, $\pm e_1, \dots, \pm e_d$). That said, we should clarify that this formula was *derived* in earlier work, so it represents a known mathematical relationship now applied here.

This study investigates the influence of quantum corrections on the high-frequency chirp-signal quasinormal modes associated with Schwarzschild-black-hole inspirations, utilizing the perturbation equation for the radial Teukolsky component. These quantum modifications manifest as adjustments to the black hole's effective mass, parameters of the angular momentum, and the spin. Numerical results indicate that incorporating these quantum corrections alters the complex frequencies of high-frequency QNMs in the extreme mass ratio limit. Specifically, when the black hole spin is antialigned with the spin of the smaller body, the real components of these frequencies are diminished; conversely, if the spin is aligned, they are augmented. Furthermore, at the same high-frequency regime, the quantum contributions lead to reductions in the imaginary parts of these modes' complex frequencies.

This study investigates thermodynamic properties and equation of state for an equilibrium quantum system composed of massless Dirac fermions enclosed within a container of volume $V$. Assuming the container exhibits smooth, closed boundaries with a total area $\Sigma$ and volume $V$, the analysis derives exact expressions—valid across all temperatures and chemical potentials—for energy, entropy, pressure, heat capacity, and the specific heat behavior. While pressure and heat capacity follow standard laws, the heat capacity reveals a distinct non-standard term characteristic of three-dimensional boundaries, scaling as $T^2/\sqrt{V}$. Unlike the bulk contribution consistent with Stefan-Boltzman law, this surface term dominates the heat capacity at high temperatures or extreme degeneracy. A significant finding is that the surface contribution to heat capacity scales inversely with the square root of volume, implying that larger systems exhibit relatively greater surface-induced heat capacity. The surface contribution vanishes only under conditions of zero volume, infinite volume, or zero temperature.

Creating speech corpus data is essential for speech synthesis; however, it is costly and labor-intensive, particularly for paragraph-length utterances which require extensive collection efforts. To circumvent these constraints, this study proposes a method to automatically generate high-quality paragraph-level synthetic speech by leveraging pre-trained neural network models. We specifically develop two key components: first, a prosody model that produces smooth, natural intonation using discrete phoneme labels; second, a voice model that maps continuous residual acoustic features directly to a given voice model. These generated synthetic voices are then evaluated against both human-recorded data and self-generated samples. The results indicate that our proposed approach not only produces superior synthetic speech quality but also maintains robust performance even when applied to existing physical recordings.

Standard projection predictive inference swaps a reference model for the target model while keeping the target's predictive distribution intact. Although this facilitates selection in large models with numerous covariates, the typical algorithms are model-specific, rendering their extension to complex structures like graphical models or those incorporating random effects unfeasible. Addressing this gap, we generalize projection predictive inference to these complex settings. The core methodology involves selecting projections that maintain the target model's distributional properties. For scenarios where the target is a Gaussian process, we offer a closed-form solution; the paper also introduces an adaptable algorithm capable of handling models that are not strictly closed-form. These contributions allow us to visualize the learning process and understand how predictors shape results within complex frameworks. Empirical testing across various contexts demonstrates that these projection selection strategies effectively distinguish target from noise models and reliably capture the underlying data-generating process.

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have proven highly effective across numerous domains, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where minimal, often imperceptible perturbations can cause significant performance degradation. This paper explores the generation of such adversarial examples using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to learn a mapping from latent space to adversarial sample distribution. By integrating a discriminator evaluation of sample realism with a variational autoencoder (VAE) framework, we enable optimization within the latent manifold. Evaluation on MNIST and FashionMNIST confirms that the proposed approach successfully crafts adversarial instances for both native and transferred scenarios outperforming established methods.

This study examines how the sharing dynamics of conspiracy theories unfold within climate change contexts on X (formerly Twitter). Through an analysis of a large dataset of conspiracy-related tweets and their associated metadata, the research explores how perceived levels of support for the conspiracy influence (1) an individual's conspiracy-sharing activity and (2) the collective impact of others' belief levels on that individual's behavior. Findings indicate that perceived belief levels significantly affect both concepts. First, users with stronger belief levels tend to share conspiracies more frequently than those with weaker levels. Second, the aggregate belief environment surrounding a user substantially impacts their own sharing volume, regardless of their initial belief level. Furthermore, the study addresses the role of conspiracy recipients in these dynamics, observing that both believers and skeptics engage in sharing activities. Crucially, it is found that others' reactions play a significant part in determining sharing frequencies, with evidence suggesting that receiving information from skeptics may actually motivate believers to disseminate conspiracy content more often.

This study reports an examination of dark matter production using proton-proton collision data recorded by the CMS experiment at the LHC during 2016, 2017, and 2018, analyzing events with a single photon and substantial missing transverse momentum in proton-proton collisions. The analysis targets events featuring a single photon and significant missing transverse momentum, targeting the discovery of scalar or pseudoscalar mediator particles coupling to dark matter via Higgs-strahlung processes involving final states of single photons, while comparing predictions to data to search for deviations. Analyses were segmented into bins based on the photon's transverse momentum, its polar angle, the magnitude of the missing transverse momentum, the number of jets, and the mass of the strahlung process (combinations of the photon and Higgs boson). Using a maximum-likelihood technique to calculate 95% confidence level limits on dark matter production cross-sections, researchers derived upper limits on dark matter cross-sections for particles with varying masses. These particles were postulated to interact via scalar, pseudoscalar, or vector mediators. The study also analyzed chiral interactions using a two-to-one dark matter ratio to calculate limits on coupling constants. No statistically significant discrepancies were observed between measurements and standard model predictions.

In this paper, we present a unified framework for formulating the Auslander-Reiten n-exangle that corresponds to the classical, dimension-shifting duality of Ausleven and Rees between projective and injective modules. This framework also clarifies the definition of an exangulated category as proposed by Nakaoka and Palu. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if $\mathcal{E}$ is a Krull-Schmidt exangulated category featuring an admissible $\mathcal{E}$-exact sequence decomposition and satisfying the test ideal condition, then $\mathcal{E}$ exhibits an Ausladen-Reiten n-exangle if and only if it is homologically $n$-Frobenius with respect to its associated auto-equivalence. Additionally, we investigate the preservation of these n-exangles under quotient operations within the category $\mathcal{E}$.

Building on Beatty, Chen, and Scott (2019), this paper expands the existing no-interaction model by introducing instruments for several unrelated (unordered) treatments. The proposed framework permits positive first-stage correlations among these instruments, accommodating scenarios where treatment interactions are conditionally orthogonal relative to treatment effects. We propose consistent estimators for parameters that describe joint treatment effects and interaction structures, providing explicit standard errors that isolate a minimal set of identifying assumptions. The estimation approach relies on solving systems of linear equations generated by zero-expectation conditions on suitable score functions. Flexible score functions grant freedom in modeling treatment effect heterogeneity, allowing for distinct parametric, semi-parametric, or nonparametric strategies. The paper demonstrates that treatment effects remain robust to misspecification regarding treatment interactions. Furthermore, we utilize data from a randomized field experiment involving college students to evaluate treatment responses to three separate interventions.

Creating antimatter is a formidable challenge, largely due to the minute yields resulting from production processes. While ion colliders have recently made significant strides in generating high quantities of high-energy antiprotons and antideuterons, employing these low-velocity antimatter particles for scattering experiments remains difficult. The detection method relies on identifying characteristic peaks of scattering maxima (often called Feshbach resonances) within the energy-dependent optical potential's real component. To determine this optical potential, one must measure how phase shifts vary with energy; however, because of the extremely low interaction rates associated with low velocities, conducting such measurements is extremely difficult. This paper proposes an innovative technique for determining the strong interaction potential through "antibullets"—using antideuterons as projectiles—and demonstrates that the depth of the potential's real component can be derived from the scattering maximum's energy, while its imaginary component is obtained from the measured total reaction cross-section.

Accretion onto young stars within multiple systems offers a unique perspective on the formation of multiple planets and stars. Recent observations of multiple accretion shocks in T Tauri systems have highlighted a key question: do all members accrete equally, or are differential accretion rates at play? In this study, we examine the "differential accretion" model within hierarchical triple star systems. Our findings indicate that if the mechanism relies on orbital resonances, differential accretion is unlikely to occur in systems where the mass ratio of the small binary to the third body is less than 0.1. Conversely, if the process is driven by chaos, the most chaotic trajectories tend to funnel more shock material onto the two inner bodies than on the outermost one. Our models also reveal that the "Kozai-Lidov" oscillation scenario, previously thought to facilitate differential accretation, is not a viable explanation for observed shock signatures. Consequently, the accretion shocks detected in T Tauri systems likely indicate that at least two members of the system are actively accreting.

We examine intrinsically flat spacetimes that exhibit symmetry under the group $ISO(2,1)$, which represents the isometry group of the Minkowski space in two dimensions combined with translations. This class encompasses all previously identified flat cosmological models and extends to solutions where the metric displays periodicity along one coordinate. Given that the only invariant structures definable by the group are the co-variant trivial ones, we adopt the co-variant trivialization to express the coefficients of the line element. By employing an appropriate coordinate transformation, these trivial coefficients are systematically eliminated; specifically, up to three integration constants, the resulting metrics are shown to be intrinsically equivalent to zero-curved forms reported in existing literature. Furthermore, we demonstrate the unjustified and misleading nature of certain claims found on the internet which suggest that these universal solutions could serve as simplified models for the expanding universe.

Model composition is a fundamental technique in deep learning, leveraging existing networks to train or initialize new ones. Although this approach has been widely adopted, most related efforts focus on simple element-wise combinations like addition or concatenation, failing to leverage the full potential of model composition. In this work, we propose a straightforward yet effective strategy for composing models by emulating graph nodes within a neural network. Specifically, we incorporate an input model as a new layer and employ a small gateway layer to filter and rearrize its output features. This method successfully bridges model segments separated by a bottleneck and requires minimal extra parameters relative to the larger models involved. We validate the approach by training a segmentation network with a mid-level representation bottleneck using a restored version fed into the model. Our results demonstrate that a segmentation architecture augmented with this multi-composition layer achieves superior performance on segmentation tasks compared to single, unconstrained models. Furthermore, this technical innovation offers a valuable secondary advantage: the generated bottleneck features can be utilized for unsupervised or self-supervised learning purposes.

The masses and spins of black holes powering Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) can be deduced from their electromagnetic spectra due to the unique environments these black holes inhabit. This paper proposes a spectral modeling strategy utilizing synthetic time-series data that incorporates realistic noise levels. We introduce a deep neural network trained on simulated light curves—generated via Monte Carlo walks through AGN systems—with the specific capability to unconvolutedly recover parameters hidden within the noisy observations. This trained model subsequently analyzes real-world light curve data from AGN, successfully deriving robust estimates for black hole mass and spin.

This document describes an open-source software platform designed for neuromorphic system design, development, and testing. Leveraging over ten years of experience building custom neuromorphic hardware prototypes at Washington University in St. Louis, our team created this suite of tools to lower the barrier to entry for both current and future researchers. By allowing rapid, free, and accessible simulation on new and established designs, the platform aims to decrease the time and effort typically needed to develop and deploy neuromorphic systems. Specifically, it offers a highly customizable, free, and rapid-to-update software environment. Its parameters are easily adjustable to accommodate the evolving needs of emerging designs, and its cost-effectiveness eliminates licensing fees, thereby making it significantly more accessible than competing commercial simulators.

Solar type-I noise storms are caused by beams of accelerated electrons accelerated within flaring regions. This study examines a specific storm on September 10, 2017, linked to a microflare, which displays two distinct evolutionary modes in its source parameters: (1) a gradual mode and (2) a pulsating mode. Both are attributed to post-flare loop arcades; the gradual mode corresponds to single loops with narrow altitude profiles, while the pulsating mode results from wide arc arcs with broader altitude distributions. The findings suggest that the pulsating characteristics arise because the broad distribution of loop altudes creates corresponding fluctuations in the magnetic field that the accelerating electrons experience.

A magneto-optical trap (MOT) is a fundamental instrument in atomic physics, frequently employed to gather and chill neutral atoms using laser light. As a cost-effective technique, it facilitates numerous subsequent procedures, such as creating ultra-cold samples for optical lattice experiments or filling atomic clocks. Despite its widespread utility, detailed knowledge of a MOT's specific characteristics is often assumed rather than empirically verified, particularly for students and early-career researchers. This lack of awareness can hinder the efficient design and execution of complex atomic apparatuses. To address this, we have developed a data acquisition system capable of analyzing various aspects of a standard alkali atom MOT in diverse configurations. By utilizing a single, readily accessible optical component to split a probe beam into multiple paths, our setup generates several simultaneous measurements with minimal extra complexity. The divided probe beams interact separately with the trapped cloud, allowing for the concurrent collection of fluorescence intensity, absorption data, and first-order derivative signals. These real-time results feed into a visual interface that plots the intensity profile across the beam, enabling researchers to readily infer critical MOT parameters such as atom count, atomic mass density distribution, and atomic velocity spread.

We investigate the accretion of a spherical cloud of identical particles onto a non-rotating black hole, where the cloud possesses specific values for surface density and angular momentum. By solving Newtonian equations of motion, we calculate the time-dependent mass accretion rate $\dot{M}(t)$ and demonstrate that it converges to a steady state. This derived $\dot{M}(t)$ is then compared with predictions from the General Relativity framework. The findings reveal strong agreement between the relativistic and Newtonian models regardless of whether the cloud is bound or expanding. Additionally, we calculate the spin parameter of the resulting Kerr black hole and determine the corresponding horizon radii.

We investigate the probabilities of both prompt and delayed free-space atoms' emission after excitation in proximity to a conducting plane. This study addresses the influence of quantum vacuum fluctuations, initially inducing complex excited states that decay promptly; however, it highlights that delayed emission can also occur. Our findings indicate that the probability of this prompt emission is impacted by the distance between the plane and the free-space atom, as well as its orientation relative to the surface.

The ongoing debate regarding whether massive stars form within dense clusters or in isolation has persisted for decades. Recent observations of young, single O- and B-type stars located in low-density regions suggest two possibilities: either such stars do form in clusters and migrate outward, or isolation is a viable formation channel. This study addresses these possibilities by analyzing the spatial distribution of stars younger than 8 million years across four distinct environments—two clusters (NGC 6611 and NGC 6334) and two ORION-CLOUD regions (ORION-CMF and ORION-KM4)—utilizing data from the Gaia DR2 mission. By comparing the positional distributions of O- and B-type stars in these diverse settings, we found that the areas outside the core density of the clusters overlap significantly with the generic star-forming clouds. This spatial correlation indicates that at least a portion of the massive stars found in sparse outer regions originated in the cluster centers and subsequently migrated outward due to dynamic interactions, a conclusion further supported by our findings regarding the age distribution of these stars.

This study addresses a normalized ground state eigenpair associated with a specific biharmonic Choquard problem. By applying variational methods to the problem at hand, we establish the necessary existence results. Additionally, future research could explore related non-local or higher-dimensional phenomena.

Handwritten document images frequently undergo degradation due to factors like poor lighting, aging documents, and substandard scanning techniques, which compromise their clarity and hinder their utility for digital archiving and data processing. Although numerous image enhancement methods have been developed for general photographic applications, they often fail under specific handwriting conditions. This study introduces a deep learning-based restoration framework tailored to elevate the quality of handwritten documents. We propose a multi-scale architecture that integrates a multi-scale perception module and a constraint-driven multi-scale generator, supported by training on a newly created dataset of 138,954 image pairs covering various handwriting styles and degradation artifacts. Evaluations utilizing PSNR, SSIM, and three deep-learning metrics, alongside comparisons with current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrate the model's superior effectiveness in recovering degraded handwritten documents.

Although Optical Character Recognition (OCR) has become a widely used technology for converting visual inputs into machine-readable text, existing systems often lack robust performance when processing linear barcodes and machine zone annotation (MZA) found on ID cards. To address this specific challenge, we have developed and released the open-source card-Ober-OCR Python library. This system integrates multiple specialized components, including pre-processing, state-of-the-art line OCR, MZA detection, and orientation strategies, along with post-processing modules.

This paper introduces an innovative nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA) framework designed specifically for high-mobility vehicular networks. At the core of our proposal is an advanced channel tracking mechanism that leverages the characteristics of clustered channel responses and an non-linear extended Kalman filter. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the viability of this NOMA framework and confirm that the proposed tracking method significantly surpasses conventional non-ordered pilot strategies, particularly when utilizing a limited quantity of pilot signals. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that increasing pilot density enhances overall channel tracking precision and lowers the probability distribution regarding significant tracking errors. Ultimately, our results affirm that the proposed NOMA communication paradigm combined with robust channel tracking is well-suited for next-generation 5G systems.

Automated RGB colorization has become increasingly popular due to its practical applications and cost-effectiveness; however, achieving high-quality results remains difficult because of ambiguities in missing chromatic information, which this study seeks to address. By analyzing textures and shapes via visual perception theories, the paper proposes a novel method incorporating a spatial channel network and a color harmony generation module. The former extracts features for basic color prediction, while the latter creates aesthetically pleasing hue and saturation variations based those extracts. Evaluations on two public datasets, color363-128k-1 and Color177777-1 and Color2 million, demonstrate that this enhanced architecture outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

We introduce a scheme grounded in the Network Lifting Theorem for determining Artificial Neural Network weights, enabling the computation of equivalent single-hidden layer networks that maintain the exact representation of deeper, original architectures. This method constructs a sparsely connected network of depth two, where training involves optimizing only these shallow weights to mirror the input-output mappings of the initial deep network, and demonstrates that minimizing a Minkowski $p$-norm for $p > 1$ ensures resulting equivalent networks remain sparsely connected.

Additionally, the panel created the ECFA Newsletter and launched an information portal. This document outlines the group's founding composition and outlines its established procedures.

Learning from Demonstration (LfD) has emerged as a robust, general-purpose framework for teaching cognitive robotic tasks, enabling the acquisition of abilities like scene understanding, object categorization, and action generation by analyzing human videos. Multi-agent learning extends this concept by leveraging knowledge shared among multiple agents to master complex skills, thereby emulating collaborative human behavior. This paper reviews the convergence of these two areas and explores potential future trajectories. We outline key technological barriers in vision, cognition, and locomotion, along with corresponding strategies to overcome them. Finally, by synthesizing existing approaches, we highlight promising avenues for advancing cognitive robotics through the integration of learning from demonstration with multi-agent systems.

A bias-reduced estimator for the population-level mean is developed to decrease the bias in a high-dimensional median-regression framework, where the relationship between continuous outcomes and high-dimensional covariates is captured using smooth, nonparametric check-functions. This new bias-reduced estimator enhances existing bias-correcting methods by eliminating the need for an auxiliary correction step, allowing variance estimation and hypothesis testing without further adjustment. We demonstrate that this approach possesses desirable theoretical properties, including \(\ell_2\)-consistency, the bias-stabilization property, asymptotic normality, and complete bias-stabilization. Furthermore, we introduce a scalable bias-reduced estimator through Lasso regularization and validate its efficacy using both fabricated and real empirical to demonstrate performance improvements.

Relation extraction (RE) aims to retrieve the connections between entities in text, a task critical for applications like knowledge base population. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have recently outperformed Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) in many NLP applications, the specific advantages of CNNs over RNNs in the context of RE remain under investigation. This study examines these benefits within RE to guide future research. We also evaluate various RE datasets to contrast RE with other Named Entity Recognition and Joint Entity-Relation Extraction tasks, highlighting the distinctions in performance across these tasks.

We present a high-dimensional generalization of the anti-\textit{text}i-quarkonium number density within the framework of kinetic theory. Our framework constructs an isotropically local equilibrium distribution for the scattering integral and incorporates specific integrands for both isotropic vector and anisotropic vector forms. Consequently, we derive corresponding equilibrium number densities for the first orders up to N dimensions under various types of integrability assumptions. Our findings demonstrate that increasing the dimensionality raises the dissociation temperature of quarkonium, with results for the isotropic case aligning perfectly with expectations up to 7 dimensions. Furthermore, anisotropy leads to a decreased dissociation temperature; however, this effect becomes negligible in higher-dimensional spaces.

This study employs muon-spin rotation and relaxation methods to explore the magnetic characteristics of the mixed-valence compound Tb$_3$RuO$_7$. Evidence suggests Ru ions exist in both +3 and +4 oxidation states, contributing to the complex interplay between Kondo effects and long-range ordering. Below the critical temperature of 15 K, the system exhibits a complex ordered structure where the Ru$_1$ and Ru$_2$ moments display opposite temperature dependencies in their magnitudes. At 2 K, the Tb and Ru$_1$ moments reach substantial values of 6.55(2) $\mu$_B and 1.35(2) $\mu$_B, respectively, whereas the Ru$_2$ moment remains significantly smaller at 0.55(2) $\mu$_B. Furthermore, the observed freeze-in of oscillating NMR signals around 15 K supports the interpretation that the system exists in a mixed-valence state.

This study introduces a novel method for signal representation applicable to images and videos, utilizing a dual-MLP framework consisting of two multilayer perceptrons. The first network handles coordinate mapping, while the second manages the signal mapping. Together, these components enable the continuous extension of images and videos into the high-dimensional space. We detail how this approach facilitates the reconstruction of content at missing coordinates, supporting applications in image completion and video filling. Furthermore, we recover the inverse transformation—mapping from high-dimensional space back to the original domain. Experiments on standard datasets validate the technique, with the resulting signals demonstrating significant potential for downstream tasks, including classification. Relevant source code is accessible via the provided link.

While most existing techniques for covariate shift adaptation combine adaptation with semi-supervised learning using only unlabeled data, this work introduces a new approach that incorporates selection labels instead. Additionally, only a small portion of the unlabeled dataset is selected for adaptation training, not all of it. Despite this seemingly disadvantage compared to using full datasets, our method yields superior performance. Unlike current adaptation approaches, this technique includes a selection mechanism to identify informative samples for both labeled and unlabeled data, a strategy supported by theoretical analysis. Empirical evaluations on multiple real-world datasets across various domains demonstrate that Sample Selection Adaptation (SSA) consistently outperforms both standard adaptation methods and those using all unlabeled data via semi-supervised learning with lower unlabeled data amounts.

Recent research in rational analysis has investigated the relationships between the behavior of deep learning models and the geometry of their underlying systems. For instance, researchers have explored how the distribution of activations across a model's layers correlates with the distribution of neural tangents or the spectrum of the training data. In this work, we extend this line of inquiry by examining the rational structures inherent in both the input space and the high-dimensional manifold embedded within a model's layers. By adapting the concept of a data manifold to reflect reality more accurately, we establish logical connections between model architecture and layer-wise geometry, demonstrating that the successive layers of a model approximate the principal components of the layer below it. This reasoning further supports existing observations regarding the distribution of model weights and offers explanations for the empirical phenomenon known as "parallelism" across deep model layers.

This paper addresses \cite{weil}\'s query regarding $h^+$, Ambert\'s \cite{ambert} question concerning $h_R$, and investigates the origins of highly positive primes within arbitrary number fields. The author establishes Ambert\'s conjecture for quadratic fields and proves that for numbers field containing at least one ramified inertial prime, both $h^+$ and $h_R$ are bounded solely as a function of the maximal degree $t$ of these primes. Furthermore, the text presents the first explicit bound for the strictly Regis-Ribault invariant in fields of degree $t$. The work concludes with a comprehensive analysis of the asymptotic behavior and distribution patterns across the families of values for primitive ambiguous principal ideals, as well as general related invariants.

This study introduces a novel architecture for Deep Neural Network (DNN) classifiers within jet substructure, leveraging an attention mechanism to integrate expert variables as side information. Our approach posits that learned associations between jet properties and classification tasks can enhance classification efficacy. Consequently, we partition the network into two components: an expert subnetwork and a main network. The expert subnetwork processes individual jet properties, while the main network consists of an attention module and a classification layer. Within the attention module, we compute relevance scores for each expert using the main network's intermediate activations, effectively weighting their contributions. These scores facilitate the aggregation of weighted expert embeddings, which are then fused with the main network's features for final classification. We evaluated this method on two datasets: the FCC Jet Physics dataset and LHC Run 2 Jet properties dataset, focusing specifically on b-tagging and W-tagging. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed DNN structure consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, analyses of side-information relevance align with our initial hypothesis, confirming that feature importance varies depending on the specific tagging task.

For every positive integer r, the r-associated Stirling number of the second kind quantifies partitions of the collection {1, ..., n} where no block has a size exceeding r. In this work, we introduce generalizations of elementary symmetric functions and power sum symmetric functions specifically tailored for r, subsequently determining various identities for these structures.

This study introduces the development of C++ classes designed to facilitate symbolic manipulation within layer groups, a specialized subset of space groups that allow horizontal mirrors. By integrating with the *symbint* library for symbolic computation and *fputil* for floating-point operations, the software leverages the efficiency of these established tools. *symbint* specifically supports the robust algebraic operations required to handle symmetries in computational solid-state physics. Building on this foundation, the presented implementation enables precise and rapid calculation of various layer group attributes, including conjugacy classes, element counts by class, fixed points, and rotation axes.

This work introduces a class of first-order differential operators that generalize the concept of flat-plane momentum and establish associated quantum dynamics. These intrinsically defined momentum operators exhibit a non-vanishing commutator, with the resulting coupling dependent on the geometry of the underlying intrinsically curved manifolds; specifically, it corresponds to the sectional curvature for 2-manifolds and the mean curvature scalar for loop spaces. Consequently, the relations constitute a non-volatile model of the Uncertainty Principle driven by spacetime curvature. The operators admit well-defined, Hermitian adjoints, ensuring self-adjointness and unitary evolution. The dependence of the uncertainty relations on geometry is explicit: in dimensions greater than two, such as for surfaces or higher, the specific nature of the non-commuting terms reflects either sectional or mean curvature, respectively. The paper begins by detailing the construction of these canonical intrinsically defined momentum operators. The section concludes by deriving an explicit expression for the time-dependent state vector $\psi(t)$ governed by the Dirac equation.

Deforming the integration contours offers a method to alleviate the sign problem encountered by Monte Carlo simulations away from half-filling. However, the resulting Jacobian determinant within the Boltzmann weight limits generic neural network applications, as their associated computational cost typically scales cubically with volume. By introducing an architecture grounded in complex-valued affine coupling layers instead, we diminish this overhead to linear scaling. The effectiveness of this approach is validated across various system sizes, including one too vast for traditional Monte Carlo techniques owing to its intense sign problem.

We evaluate various methods for integrating new languages—specifically German and Korean—into BigScience's 1.3-billion parameter multilingual pre-trained model. This model originally supports 13 languages. The research examines how different factors influence language adaptation performance and assesses the tradeoffs between computational resources and anticipated results.

This research introduces the m-arbitrary FastICA Fastico algorithm (m-ar-K-Fastica) as an enhanced approach for feature extraction that integrates the modified domain approach into traditional dataICA. While FastICA is widely recognized for its efficacy in solving linear blind source problems, its performance degrades with randomness; our proposed method addresses this limitation. The dm transformation allows the algorithm to project complex characteristics onto real structures, where standard fast algorithm steps are applied to solve the problem. Experimental results indicate that this method enhances feature extraction performance, particularly in scenarios involving arbitrary data. Additionally, the study validates that these extracted features effectively support subsequent classification processes using various classifiers.

This paper expands on previous research by demonstrating that if Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) can distinguish non-isomorphic pairs within a class of graphs, then a non-trivial separation also exists within bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus. This finding constitutes the dual direction of a non-standard complexity theorem previously established by Biere and Pichler. The current work further clarifies the relationship between CPT and bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus by proving that any non-CPT invariant detectable in bounded-degree extended polynomial time for a graph class admits a non-trational non-CPT refutation in resolution. Similarly, the argument is reversed: the existence in CPT of a refutation for a non-CPT refutable argument implies the ability to distinguish a non-isomorphic pair that non-CPT time cannot separate. All demonstrations hold for any graph class lacking hereditary properties.

An associated concept for any linked set $G$ within a ring $R$ is its *cover number*, denoted $\sigma(G)$, representing the minimal cardinality of a subset $K$ (where $K \subset G$) capable of anti-generating $G$. This study offers a thorough analysis of the cover numbers for various ideal collections in rings utilizing $p$-adic analysis tools for their quantification via topological properties. We explore these cover numbers in both finite and infinite commutative rings that possess finitely many or a finite number of associated ideals. Additionally, we analyze these measures for chains and partially ordered sets of ideals situated in associative rings.

Social media generates content at a deluge rate, creating a pressing need to verify claims by cross-referencing established fact bases. This paper introduces a two-tiered architecture designed to integrate real-time user-generated data with fact-verification workflows and the fact-verse. The proposed system consists of two primary components: (1) *F-Verse*, which serves as a knowledge-intensive database for managing fact-checking operations, and (2) *VeriCheck*, a service layer offering integrated APIs for interacting with that system. This architecture streamlines the complexity of managing dynamic fact verification, providing developers with straightforward mechanisms to incorporate verification capabilities into diverse applications. The paper concludes with a survey of available open-source solutions, their use cases, and developing standards regarding fact-verification APIs.

The surge in high-dimensional, sparse, and unstructured real-world events on social platforms has driven a demand for data-driven detection methods. These events, such as natural disasters, political elections, or celebrity weddings, generate massive volumes of user posts regarding shared experiences. We propose a new supervised learning framework that integrates specialized neural network components to automatically extract meaningful features from stream data for event detection. To our knowledge, this represents the first end-to-end trainable system of its kind. We have also established the first large-scale public dataset containing over 2.5 million verified event instances for testing. Comprehensive experiments on this new dataset, as well as comparisons with baseline methods using standard benchmark data, demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods across all evaluated metrics.

We introduce a conceptually straightforward yet mathematically robust approach to cosmological parameter estimation that leverages the 3D positions of galaxies and the cosmic web. This method utilizes what is termed the "weighted skew-spectrum," defined in Fourier space as the three-point correlation function multiplied by the galaxy power spectrum. By probing both the large and small scales, this formulation offers an elegant intermediary to bridge the gaps between configuration and Fourier spaces. This balance provides significant computational advantages over traditional real-space estimators, such as the correlation function, while delivering greater resilience against nonlinear effects than standard k-space techniques, specifically the galaxy power spectrum.

Having demonstrated the method's efficacy through simulations, we verified its $f_{\rm virion}$ recovery across various bias levels and demonstrated that it accurately extracts information from the small-scale regime. Using 20 million mock quasar positions up to $z=2.4$, which were calibrated with bias parameters derived from an $LF_{\rm dim}$ analysis, the resulting estimators achieve near-optimal variance. This performance rivals that of the optimal estimator derived from the 30 million $Z_{\rm survey}$ quasar positions at $h=10 h^{-1}$ Mpc, a conclusion further supported by convergence tests.

By viewing adversarial training as a Bayesian inference problem, we introduce BAdvTr, a principled framework that unifies model learning and the derivation of uncertainty-aware test-time defenses. Traditional adversarial training relies on the inefficient and approximate worst-case scenario; in contrast, BAdvTR employs the more efficient most-likely approach grounded in the posterior distribution of the model. This shift not only matches the adversarial threat model but also enhances robustness by accounting for prediction uncertainty. Empirical results demonstrate that BAdvTr significantly improves upon existing adversarial training techniques, achieving superior performance with approximately 55% less data, 35% less wall-clock training time, and reduced memory requirements compared to the standard.

Beginning in January 2020, the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic has resulted in hundreds of thousands of fatalities and the widespread dissemination of misinformation, particularly during the Wuhan outbreak. This study examines the rumor network using only data accessible to the general public, aiming to determine its structural characteristics and the influence of related factors on its expansion. By applying appropriate methodologies, this work analyzes the rumor network's topology alongside the relationship between its spread and public sentiment. The study concludes by suggesting effective mitigation strategies.

This paper addresses the classification of hyperspectral images through dimensionality reduction, a strategy designed to lower computational costs and memory requirements. The study evaluates four reduction techniques: Principal Component Analysis, Linear Discriminant Analysis, and two linear manifold learning methods, specifically Laplacian and Riemannian PCA. Experiments were conducted using four public datasets, and results indicate that both the reduction rate and the compression rate significantly impact classification accuracy. The Riemannian PCA method, applied with a fixed reduction rate, was determined most effective at balancing computational efficiency and accuracy. Consequently, experiments focused on varying the compression rate within this method. These tests involved setting different numbers of principal components via linear discriminant analysis to compress the imagery, followed by classification using a Bayesian, neural network, and a k-nearest neighbor algorithm. The findings demonstrate that a higher compression rate can actually enhance classification accuracy. Consequently, employing linear discriminant analysis, Riemannian PCA, and a neural network emerged as an optimal configuration, offering the best trade-off between processing speed and accuracy.

Despite their exceptional performance on numerous practical challenges, neural networks often suffer from excessive complexity, comprising numerous redundant components. To address this, network pruning has emerged as a vital technique for refining models by eliminating superfluous parts. Guided by the "lottery ticket hypothesis," which posits that small, sparse subnetworks can match the accuracy of larger networks, research has concentrated on extracting these subsets. This study evaluates various pruning strategies for computer vision tasks using ResNet architectures. Our comprehensive analysis covers different pruning approaches, looks into the effects of network width versus depth removal, and investigates the influence of top-level vs intermediate node selection. Based on this rigorous investigation, we offer practical guidelines to enhance pruning outcomes in computer vision contexts.

This study introduces ProCS, the inaugural tool designed to predict protein-specific amide proton chemical shifts using deep residual convolutional neural networks. As proteins serve as fundamental units of life, with their biological roles dictated by structural features, this work aims to extract structural insights from amide proton resonance data. While such data is abundant, its structural potential has remained largely untapped due to a lack of effective prediction methodologies. By integrating amino acid sequences directly into the model, ProCS generates structural models that are robust and resistant to overfitting, obviating the need for traditional structural augmentation or engineering. Validated on a hold-out dataset of 1,045 proteins, ProCS achieved a mean $R^2$ value of 0.975 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.435 ppm. When compared to the state-of-the-art method, it demonstrated significant improvements, delivering more than double the magnitude of gain in terms of RMSE efficiency. Furthermore, the model exhibits stability and generalization across diverse protein families, even those absent from baseline training datasets. These results underscore deep convolutional neural networks as powerful instruments for structural biology, capable of unlocking valuable structural information hidden within amino acid sequences.

The loss function is vital for deep neural network (DNN) training in supervised tasks like classification. Although the cross-entropy loss is the standard choice, recent research explores alternatives. This work experimentally evaluates various losses—including cross-entropy, hinge loss, and others—for predicting images from microscopy data. Findings show that some alternative losses match or exceed cross-entropy's accuracy, particularly when combined with curriculum learning. Additionally, specific losses proved more robust to the learning rate, a conclusion supported by the observation that certain losses minimize gradients across training batches more effectively than others.

Investigating collective phenomena demands accurate handling of multi-particle correlations, which can be significantly streamlined by decoupling techniques; however, such approaches fail when correlations inherently remain strongly coupled. The parquet theory offers a robust solution in this scenario, yet its computational complexity has previously precluded more than a two-dimensional implementation. This limitation is addressed in our current work, which achieves four-dimensional parquet solvability for spin systems by exploiting modern variational matrix product states (matrix product states) to intelligibly partition the complex many-spin structure. Implemented within a pole-resummed tensor network framework, our strategy efficiently manages dominant diagonal long-range order contributions. We validate this methodology by analyzing antiferromagnetic spin-1/2 squares in a magnetic field, comparing our results against both diagonal and non-diagonal analytically tractable long-term behaviors.

The phase transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator manifests as the splitting of excitonic energy gaps. By applying exact diagonalization to the one- and two-dimensional Toy Model, we establish the critical coupling constant ($\lambda_{d}^{*}$) where this transition occurs; this parameter quantifies the attractive electron-hole interaction strength. The lower bound estimate for $\lambda_{d}^{*}$ is improved by employing a mean-field path integral approach, which incorporates nonlocal correlations of the auxiliary field. Incorporating these effects lowers the estimated lower bound for $\lambda_{d}^{*}$ and thereby raises the upper bound, with the resulting theoretical estimates for the transition shown to align with experimental observations in transition-metal dichalcogenides monolayers.

Although recent years have seen the proliferation of safety reporting platforms, their success in mitigating crime remains questionable. Research suggests these platforms fail to achieve optimal outcomes because they neglect users' psychological and safety concerns, specifically by ignoring the emotional support needs of those using the systems. To investigate the connection between emotional care and system engagement, the study examines the interaction patterns of users within the China Net Safety Report platform. Utilizing detailed temporal reporting and textual data, the authors construct an original framework for identifying emotional states. Findings reveal a direct, positive correlation between emotional distress and reporting frequency; consequently, public officials exhibit a higher sensitivity to emotional support offers than do ordinary citizens. Drawing on these reported behaviors, the study proposes an automated support detection mechanism and evaluates its performance. The results indicate that integrating emotional support offers significantly boosts subscription subscription rates and reduces the reporting threshold. Ultimately, the study redefines the reporting phenomenon by interpreting it through the lens of an "emotional event," arguing that future platform designs must prioritize emotional关怀 (care) to enhance overall system efficacy.

This study reports experimental evidence of s-wave superconductivity in magnetically doped, exfoliated Bi$_2$Se$_3$ flower-shaped topological insulators. Using a combination of low-temperature transport measurements and high-resolution magnetoptical microscopy, we identified spontaneous broken time-reversal symmetry within the mixed spin-chiral ferromagnetic domains of CuMnAs$_2$ clusters. Our analysis indicates that the superconducting transition temperature is suppressed as magnetic ion concentration increases. Furthermore, the superconducting critical field displays a non-monotonic behavior, switching from suppression to enhancement with continued doping of Mn atoms. These findings offer new insights into the superconductor-insulator transitions observed in thin films composed of the same bi-layer Bi$_2$Se$_3$.

Active learning methodologies currently focus on either reducing uncertainty or leveraging pseudo-semantic information to determine which data points to label next, a process often repeated in an unsupervised co-training framework to enhance performance. This study introduces a novel metric known as loudness complexity, which quantifies the intricacy of audio signals by examining the fluctuations in short-term perceived loudness. By fitting these fluctuations to a generalized Archimedean copula, the formula efficiently captures the statistical dependencies inherent in short-term loudness variations. Applying this to a vast collection of one million songs from the Gramophone dataset, which spans from the 1960s to the 2000s, reveals a notable decrease in average loudness complexity over the decades. Furthermore, an analysis of over 350,000 tracks labeled as classical music indicates a consistent increase in complexity from the 1960s through the 2000s, contrasting the general trend.

This work examines a stochastic partition mechanism where numbers $1, 2, \dots$ are sequentially generated, with each new number either initiates a fresh block or adds to an existing one. The decision to create a new block when number $n$ considers joining a block of size $j$ is governed by probabilities $p_j$. Under specific conditions regarding the function $p_j$, we analyze blocks of varying sizes and counts, offering results that include weak convergence, in complete independence, order-based representations, limiting distributions, and asymptotic behavior that deviates from standard assumptions.

Penelope Mantiukliene's thesis examines the structural components of intuitionistic logic, specifically natural deduction and sequent calculus. She begins by outlining the concepts of proof theory and proof-theoretical semantics before exploring various formulations of logical systems. The focus then shifts to the inference rules of sequent calculi for intuitionistic logic, accompanied by conditions of substructural nature. The study continues with an analysis of structural properties of these systems, including inversion, contraction freedom, and the cut-elimination theorem.

The central portion of the work addresses the structural properties of intuitionistic natural deduction. Starting with the inversion principle and its significance, the thesis explores the transformation of deduction into a sequent calculus system. The discussion proceeds to formulate a translation function that maps sequent calculi into natural deduction and demonstrates a convergence theorem. This finds that, provided the function satisfies specific constraints, it acts as a simultaneous proof and reverse proof, effectively establishing logical equivalence between the two frameworks. The final section outlines several structural attributes of intuitionistic natural deduction derived from these transformations and concludes by defining the properties related to the rule of exchange.

A central challenge in reinforcement learning is crafting an effective reward function, a task often addressed through human feedback. Unfortunately, traditional methods like direct preference or configuration gathering struggle with the cognitive load they impose on annotators, becoming ineffective when tasks are intricate or require extensive prior domain knowledge. To overcome this, we introduce a crowdsourcing approach based on the acquisition of discrete knowledge facts instead. Our solution includes a novel learning algorithm designed to construct a reward function from this collection of facts. We validate our method across diverse tasks, both in controlled environments and using data from the general public, and provide a analysis of its advantages regarding annotation efficiency.

We demonstrate that a topological space $X$ has the property that its Smyth powerspace $\mathsf{Q}(X)$ is always core-compact—if and only-if $X$ itself is locally compact. Additionally, we investigate how the topological characteristics of a core-compactness of $\mathsf{Q}(X)$ impose upon $X$, establishing connections with various established topological attributes such as Hausdorff separation, countability constraints, compactness, and the regularity/regulinar regularization properties.

This work investigates a distinct class of singular vorticities in ideal planar fluid flow, merging attributes of point vortices and vortex sheets into what are known as pointed vortex loops. The analysis centers on the coadjoint orbits within the group of area-preserving diffeomorphisms for \(\mathbb{R}^2\) generated by these configurations. It is demonstrated that the corresponding polarization subgroup comprises diffeomorphisms that keep the loop invariant, thereby implying that the resulting configuration space consists solely of loops enclosing a fixed area, with no specific details provided regarding vorticity density or anchor points.

Despite counterfactual frameworks being integral to numerous econometric analyses, causal parameter estimates often remain vulnerable to biases stemming from flawed assumptions. While estimator approaches like AIPW and nAIPW boast favorable asymptotic properties, their practical performance can degrade if the targeted counterfactual framework is incorrectly specified. To address this, we introduce the DNIPW estimator, designed for robustness against the potential mis-specification of counterfactual contexts, with detailed explanations of its properties provided below.

The proposed DNIPW estimator maintains the same asymptotic advantages as its AIPW and nAIPW predecessors while extending reliability to scenarios where relevant assumptions regarding the AIPW, nAIPW, or DNIPW estimators are invalid. By leveraging the DNIPW estimator specifically for empirical analysis within the source material, researchers can enhance the robustness of their findings.

This study introduces an atmospheric circulation model built within the functional programming ecosystem of Agda. It utilizes functional recursion and pattern matching to simulate key dynamical processes driving cyclogenesis in a rotating barotropic beta-plane context. Cyclic generation depends critically on the balance between rotational effects (Coriolis force) and spatial variations in the Coriolis parameter (beta-effect) regarding the westward propagation of barotropic Rossby waves. The model demonstrates how a sinusoidal potential vorticity distribution generates cyclones through a sequence initiated by an instability in long waves. This initial wave splits into two distinct cyclonic centers positioned symmetrically around the wave's center of rotation.

Modelling extreme values is often based on asymptotic properties that yield parameterized distributions. A primary benefit of this approach is that the resulting distributional parameters remain invariant to threshold selection. In this study, we examine the asymptotic behavior of order statistics—specifically the maximums of non-i.i.d. random variables bounded above by a common upper limit. We provide specific rates of convergence for these convergences and identify conditions that accelerate them. Our analysis supports two main applications. Firstly, we propose a novel method for modelling the extremes associated with values exceeding high thresholds. Secondly, we demonstrate how this framework can estimate parameters and assess the upper bounds of calibration curves, a relationship typically observed in observational data.

This paper investigates offline reinforcement learning in continuous-state and continuous-action Markov decision processes under the assumption that an adversary has modified any arbitrary fraction of the data tuples. Our primary theoretical contribution establishes that despite such adversarial corruptions, there exists a randomized policy capable of achieving near-optimal performance with only an almost linear increase in sample complexity compared to the standard, non-corrupted setting. Leveraging this theoretical framework and supported by simulations, our experimental results demonstrate the practical application of an offline reinforcement learning algorithm that exhibits robustness against online attacks involving up to 10% tuple modifications.

This paper establishes logarithmic convexity as a consequence of the observability estimate for 1-D hyperbolic diffusion systems with dynamic boundary conditions. Based on this result, the paper proves that, for 1-D hyperbolic diffusion systems with time-delayed feedback control, the logarithmic convexity can be used to analyze the inverse problem. This approach provides the convexity estimate needed for problems involving determining unknown source terms in certain PDE models.

Although recognizing the importance of detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) samples is widely acknowledged, the community lacks consensus on their precise definition. This review examines literature published between 2017 and 2019 to address three key issues: (1) OOD detection is primarily split into semantic and methodological approaches, the former failing effectively when dealing with naturalistic shift types; (2) current evaluations are flawed due to the use of overly simplistic benchmarks that bias results toward semantic methods and favor naturalistic over non-naturalistic settings; and (3) there is a pressing need to standardize definitions, benchmarks, and evaluation metrics. Consequently, we propose revised, rigorous benchmarks covering both non-naturalistic and naturalistic shifts, along with a comprehensive evaluation protocol to better assess current OOD detection capabilities.

Recent advancements in atomic manipulation have enabled the creation and operation of various molecular machines and nanosystems, often utilizing electric currents to drive these processes as multiple individual molecules are manipulated under an optical microscope. Although current research has demonstrated multiple molecules moving in response to electrical stimuli, the specific mechanisms and efficiencies remain unquantified. In this study, we investigate the fundamental principles of these motor actions by applying a computational framework that integrates classical mechanics with quantum mechanics to analyze recent experimental data on a tested artificial molecular motor system. Our results suggest that the commonly used "ratchet" model may be inadequate and instead propose that efficient, current-driven motion stems from molecules becoming virtual "electrodes," facilitating electron tunneling between them. Furthermore, we develop simplified analytical expressions to estimate the forces acting on the molecules, offering insights into the design of future molecule-assembled nanosystems.

Origin semantics for transducers were introduced a decade ago to tackle problems in abstract syntax tree manipulation; however, only basic types have been studied until now. This work introduces and examines "destination semantics," which mirrors origin semantics in opposite direction. The paper establishes a reduction of classical language semantics to destination semantics, using this finding to contrast decidable problems under classical versus origin semantic models. It further presents a reduction of standard contextuality checks within the original semantics to Verifier contextuality within the new framework, allowing for comparable decidable problem paradigms between the two.

This paper addresses the f-Convolution problem, which involves determining all positions where a pattern function $p$ matches a function $p$ inside a domain $D$. We establish a new lower bound of $\Omega(n^{2 - \Omega(1)})$ for this problem under the assumption of conditional hypotheses. Building on this, our primary contribution is a sophisticated algorithmic framework capable of computing f-Convolution in $O(n^{2 - \Omega(1)})$ time with a complex exponent dependent on the hardness assumptions. This method unifies and broadens multiple existing techniques for various convolution and matching problems—including those involving distinct characters, linear maps, and applications in image processing and computer vision—providing improved or simplified algorithms for tasks such as correlated submatrix detection and multiple pattern matching with maps. Additionally, the introduction of this framework yields a simplified algorithm that raises the brute-force threshold for f-Convolution from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n^{4/3})$, while also yielding novel $O(n^{2 - \Omega(1)})$ solutions for $p$ with polynomially bounded outputs.

This study utilizes high-resolution near-infrared spectra to investigate the thermal structure and atmospheric composition of the K7 exoplanet GJ 229B. Spectroscopic data were gathered across the 1.0–2.5 $\mu$m wavelength range using the VLT/CRIRES and Gemini North/GMOS instruments. Data quality enhancements include a re-estimated radial velocity for the host star and improved removal of telluric absorption features. New spectral templates were generated via machine learning techniques, leveraging existing high-quality template libraries. These templates facilitate high-fidelity visual inspection and power spectrum analysis, enabling precise extraction of phase curves and identification of prominent atmospheric absorption bands. Subsequently, a statistical Bayesian thermo-chemical model was employed to analyze the phase curve data and generate spectral retrievals using HITEMP and HITRAN molecular databases. Modern retrieval methods yielded a mass of 60$^{+18}_{-10}$ M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ and an effective temperature of 630$^{+20}_{-20}$ K.
